en: [May there be auspiciousness! He who, having abandoned his primordial form, manifests in manifold ways for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world—
he whose mass of afflictions is utterly destroyed, who is like a serpent with its poison neutralized, who possesses many faces, and who is endowed with sublime enjoyments.

May that Lord of Serpents, whose body is white and stainless, who is joined in yoga and bestows yoga, whose birth is from all-knowledge, and whose constant retinue is of serpents—may he, for whom the Lord of Snakes is eternally a source of delight, protect you. (1)
[The Chapter on Concentration] Now follows the instruction on yoga.
Now, the word "atha" (now/thereupon) has the sense of introducing a topic.
It should be understood that the treatise on the instruction of yoga is here commenced.
Yoga is concentration (*samādhi*).
And that [samādhi] is a quality of the mind that is universal.
"Distracted," "dull," "distracted-and-concentrated," "one-pointed," and "restricted" are the stages of the mind.
Among these, when the mind is distracted, the samādhi that has become subordinate to distraction does not belong to the category of yoga.

However, that which illuminates the true object when the mind is one-pointed, attenuates the afflictions, loosens the bonds of karma, and brings cessation face-to-face, is called "cognitive" (*saṃprajñāta*) yoga.
We shall explain later that this consists of being accompanied by coarse discernment (*vitarka*), subtle discernment (*vicāra*), joy (*ānanda*), and the sense of "I-am-ness" (*asmitā*).
But when all mental fluctuations are suppressed, it is "non-cognitive" (*asaṃprajñāta*) samādhi.
With the desire to state its definition, this aphorism was composed:
"Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (YS 1.2).
Because no sounds are perceived, even this is designated as *saṃprajñāta-yoga*.
For the mind (*citta*) consists of the three *guṇas*, owing to its nature of luminosity (*prakhyā*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and stability (*sthiti*).
Indeed, the *sattva* of the mind, whose form is luminosity, when conjoined with *rajas* and *tamas*, becomes fond of sovereignty and sense objects.
That same [intellect], when permeated by *tamas*, becomes associated with demerit (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*), and lack of mastery (*anaiśvarya*).

That same [intellect], when the veil of delusion (*moha*) has been destroyed and it is shining forth on all sides, being permeated by a mere trace of *rajas*, becomes associated with merit (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and mastery (*aiśvarya*).

That same [intellect], when freed from even the slightest stain of *rajas* and established in its own nature, consists solely of the discriminative discernment (*anyatākhyāti*) between the intellect (*sattva*) and the self (*puruṣa*), and becomes associated with the meditation known as the "Cloud of Virtue" (*dharmamegha-dhyāna*).
Meditators call that "supreme discernment.

The power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) is unchanging, non-transmigrating, having its object revealed, pure, and infinite; it consists of the quality of *sattva*. Discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), however, is the opposite of this. Therefore, the mind, becoming detached from that [discernment], suppresses even that discernment.
In that state, it is accompanied by residual impressions (*saṃskāra*).
It is a seedless concentration (*nirbīja-samādhi*).
Because nothing whatsoever is cognized therein, it is called "without cognition" (*asaṃprajñāta*).
"That yoga is of two kinds: it is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind.

When the mind is in that state, since there is an absence of objects, what is the nature of the *puruṣa*, whose essence is the awareness of the intellect?—"At that time, the seer abides in its own nature" (Yoga Sūtra 1.3).

[YS 1.3] At that time, the power of consciousness (citiśakti) is established in its own nature, as it is in the state of liberation (kaivalya). However, while the mind is in a state of emergence (vyutthāna), although it exists in that same way, it does not exist in that same way.
How then? Because its object has been presented— there is conformity with the mental modification in other cases [Yoga Sūtra 1.4].
During emergence, the person possesses a modification that is not distinct from those modifications of the mind.
And thus says the Sūtra: "The seeing is one alone; the seeing is indeed manifestation.
The mind, which is like a magnet, assists by its mere proximity and becomes the "own" (object) of the Lord, the Person, by virtue of being an object of sight.

Therefore, the cause of the Puruṣa’s awareness of the mental modifications is a beginningless connection. Furthermore, since the mind possesses many modifications, those which are to be restrained are "the modifications are fivefold, being either afflicted or unafflicted" (Yoga Sūtra 1.5).
[YS 1.5] Those whose cause is the afflictions (kleśa) are "afflicted" (kliṣṭa), having become the field for the accumulation of latent dispositions of karma (karmāśaya).
Those whose object is discriminative discernment (khyāti) and which oppose the mandate of the constituents (guṇa) are "non-afflicted" (akliṣṭa).
Even those that fall within a stream of afflicted [states] are non-afflicted;
even during gaps in the afflicted, they remain non-afflicted;
and during gaps in the non-afflicted, they are afflicted.
Formations of such a kind are produced by the fluctuations alone, and the fluctuations are produced by the formations;
thus the wheel of fluctuations and formations revolves incessantly.
Thus, when the mind has completed its task, it abides as if it were the Self, or it undergoes dissolution.
These are the fivefold fluctuations—both afflicted and unafflicted:
valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory. (Yoga Sūtra 1.6)
Perception, inference, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition.

Perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which is a mental modification (*vṛtti*) characterized primarily by the determination of the specific qualities of an object—consisting of both general and particular aspects—arising from the coloring of the mind by external things through the channel of the senses.
The result (*phala*) is the unqualified awareness of this mental modification by the Puruṣa.
We shall establish later that the Puruṣa is the perceiver.

Inference (*anumāna*) is a cognitive process whose primary function is the determination of a universal, having as its object a relationship that follows after things of the same class and is excluded from things of a different class regarding the object to be inferred.
For example: "The moon and stars possess motion because they reach another location, like Caitra; and the Vindhya mountain lacks motion because it does not reach another location.

Valid testimony (*āgama*) is the cognitive process of a listener arising from a word, wherein an object—either perceived or inferred by a reliable person (*āpta*)—is communicated through speech in order to transfer one's own understanding to another.
That scripture whose speaker is untrustworthy because he has not perceived or inferred the object [of his teaching] is subject to error.
However, when the original speaker has perceived or inferred the object, it would be free from error.
"Error" (viparyaya) is false knowledge (mithyājñāna) which is not established in the true nature of that [object]. (Yogasūtra 1.8)
[YS 1.8] Why is that not a valid means of knowledge?
Because it is sublated by a valid means of knowledge.
Because a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) has as its object an actual reality (bhūtārtha),
it is observed that a non-valid cognition is sublated by a valid one.
For example, the perception of two moons is sublated by the perception of a single moon, which has a real object.
This ignorance consists of five sections:
ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live; these are the afflictions (*kleśa*).
By their own specific names, they are called darkness (*tamas*), delusion (*moha*), great delusion (*mahāmoha*), gloom (*tāmisra*), and utter darkness (*andhatāmisra*).
These will be discussed in connection with the impurities of the mind.
"Conceptual construction (vikalpa) is that which follows upon verbal knowledge and is devoid of an objective reality" (YS 1.9).
It does not conform to valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
nor does it conform to error (*viparyaya*).
Even though it is devoid of a real object (*vastuśūnyatva*), a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) is observed based on the power of verbal cognition.
For example, it is said that "consciousness is the essential nature of the Puruṣa. When consciousness itself is the Puruṣa, then what is designated here by what?
And yet, such designation does occur.

Just as in the case of "Caitra’s cow," so too [in the case of] "the person is inactive" (niṣkriyaḥ puruṣaḥ), where the property of a negated entity is [asserted], one understands in "the arrow stands," "it will stand," or "it has stood" merely the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) in the sense of the cessation of motion (*gatinivṛtti*).
Likewise, regarding the statement "the person has the property of non-arising," only the mere absence of the property of arising is understood, not a property inherent to the person.

Therefore, that property is conceptually constructed, and by means of it, conventional usage occurs. Sleep is a mental modification whose objective support is the notion of non-existence (Yoga Sūtra 1.10).
[YS 1.10] And that [sleep] is a specific type of cognition, because upon waking there is a reflective awareness:
"How so? 'I slept happily.'"
My mind is serene;
it makes my wisdom confident.
I have slept poorly.
"My mind is sluggish and wanders restlessly; I have slept deeply and foolishly. My limbs are heavy; my mind is exhausted."
"It remains sluggish, as if robbed.

Indeed, this reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of one who has awakened would not exist if there were no experience of a mental state (*pratyaya*); nor would there be memories dependent upon it regarding that object.
Therefore, sleep is a specific kind of mental state.
And that [mind] must be restrained in meditative absorption (samādhi) like any other object of cognition.
Memory (smṛti) is the non-losing of an experienced object.
(Yoga Sūtra 1.11)
Does the cognition remember the cognition itself, or rather the object?
The cognition, colored by the object and manifesting in the dual form of both the grasped and the grasping, initiates a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that same nature.
That impression, when activated by its own manifestor, produces a memory of that very same form, consisting of both the grasped and the grasping.

In this context, cognition (*buddhi*) is preceded by the form of the apprehending [subject], whereas memory (*smṛti*) is preceded by the form of the apprehended [object]. And that [memory] is of two kinds: that in which the object to be remembered has been previously cultivated (*bhāvita-smartavya*), and that in which the object to be remembered has not been previously cultivated (*abhāvita-smartavya*).
In a dream, the object to be remembered has been previously experienced;
however, in the waking state, it is not so experienced.
All forms of memory arise from the experience of valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory itself.
All these modes of functioning consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Pleasure, pain, and delusion are to be explained among the afflictions:
attachment is that which underlies pleasure.
Hatred is that which lies latent within suffering;
delusion, moreover, is ignorance.
All these mental fluctuations must be restrained.
Upon their cessation, there occurs either cognitive (*saṃprajñāta*) or non-cognitive (*asaṃprajñāta*) samādhi.
Now, what is the means for their cessation?—[it is said:
"Their cessation is achieved through practice and dispassion" (YS 1.12).
[YS 1.12] The river of the mind flows in both directions; it flows toward evil and it flows toward goodness.
That which is inclined toward liberation and directed toward the object of discriminative discernment is the one that flows toward goodness.
The stream of worldly existence is prone toward saṃsāra, flows downward toward sense-objects, and carries one away with evil.
Therein, by means of dispassion, the stream of sense-objects is dammed up;
by the practice of the vision of discernment, the stream of discernment is opened. Thus, the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind depends upon both.
In that regard, effort toward steadiness is practice.
Steadiness is the state of the mind, free from fluctuations, flowing in a tranquil stream.
Effort toward that end is vigor (*vīrya*), which is enthusiasm. Practice (*abhyāsa*) is the performance of the means for its attainment with the desire to bring it to completion.
That practice, however, becomes firmly established when cultivated over a long period of time, without interruption, and with devotion. [Yogasūtra 1.14]
[YS 1.14] Practiced for a long time, practiced without interruption, and practiced with devotion—
accomplished through austerity, celibacy, knowledge, and faith— it becomes possessed of honor and becomes a firm ground.
The meaning is that by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of emergence, the object is not immediately overwhelmed.
"Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the consciousness of mastery in one who is free from thirst for objects seen or heard" (YS 1.15).

Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the state of mastery characterized by effortless non-attachment, devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted, which arises through the power of discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) even when the mind is in contact with divine or non-divine objects. This occurs for one who is free from thirst for the objects of the seen world—namely women, food, drink, and power—and who is likewise free from thirst for the objects of the heard world, such as the attainment of heaven, liberation from the body (*vaidehya*), or absorption into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*).
It is the dispassion toward the *guṇas* that follows upon the clear discernment of the *puruṣa*.
(Yoga Sūtra 1.16)

One who perceives the defects in objects seen and heard becomes dispassionate; through the practice of perceiving the Puruṣa, his intellect is nourished by the discernment resulting from that purity, and he becomes dispassionate toward the guṇas, whether their nature be manifest or unmanifest.
These two constitute dispassion (*vairāgya*).
Of these, the latter is merely the clarity of knowledge.

When this [knowledge] arises, the yogi, having attained discriminative discernment (*pratyuditakhyāti*), thinks thus: "That which was to be attained has been attained; the afflictions (*kleśa*) that were to be exhausted have been exhausted; the transition through existence (*bhavasaṃkrama*), whose joints are linked together—by the non-interruption of which one dies after being born and is born after dying—that has been severed.
Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the supreme limit of knowledge itself.
For isolation (*kaivalya*) is necessarily concomitant with this very state.
Now, one might ask: how is it that for one whose mental fluctuations have been restrained by the two means, this is called "cognitive" (*saṃprajñāta*) samādhi?—
[it is so called] because it is accompanied by the forms of reasoning (*vitarka*), reflection (*vicāra*), bliss (*ānanda*), and the sense of self (*asmitā*) [Yogasūtra 1.17].
Vitarka is the coarse mental application toward an object;
vicāra is the subtle [application].
Ānanda is joy; hlāda is delight.
The consciousness of oneness is *asmitā*.
Among these, the first type of samādhi, which is accompanied by all four [mental factors], is *savitarka* (with deliberation).
The second, devoid of deliberation, is *savicāra* (with reflection).
The third is devoid of investigation but possesses joy;
the fourth is devoid of that [joy] and consists of mere I-am-ness (asmitā).
All these concentrations possess an object of focus.
Now, as for the question of what the means and what the nature of asamprajñāta-samādhi are:
"The other [samādhi], preceded by the practice of the cognition of cessation, is that in which only residual impressions remain" (YS 1.18).
When all fluctuations have subsided, the cessation of the mind, in which only latent impressions remain, is *asamprajñāta* samādhi.
Its means is supreme detachment (*para-vairāgya*).

For practice directed toward an object is not sufficient as a means to achieve that; therefore, a thought-moment of cessation (*virāma-pratyaya*), which has no objective referent, is made the object of focus.
And that [meditation] is devoid of an object.

For when the mind, preceded by the practice of that [objectless state], becomes supportless as if it has reached non-existence, this is seedless samādhi, which is "without cognitive awareness" (asaṃprajñāta).
This indeed is of two kinds: that based on means (upāyapratyaya) and that based on existence (bhavapratyaya).
In that regard, for yogins, the means (upāya) becomes the cause;
for those who are dissolved into the bodyless or into primordial nature (videha-prakṛtilaya), existence (bhava) becomes the cause.
For the gods of Videha, existence is conditioned by their past impressions (*bhavapratyaya*).

For they, experiencing a state as if it were isolation (*kaivalya*) through a mind that employs only its own latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), pass away from that particular kind of fruition of their impressions.

Likewise, those who are absorbed in primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*) experience a state as if it were isolation when the mind, still possessing a mandate for action, is dissolved into primordial nature; this continues until the mind returns again under the influence of that mandate.
For others, the conviction regarding the means arises through faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. [YS 1.20] [YS 1.20] This is the case for yogins.
Faith is the clarity of the mind;
for it protects the practitioner like a virtuous mother.
Indeed, in one who possesses faith and seeks discernment, vigor arises.
For one who has generated energy, mindfulness becomes established. When mindfulness is established, the mind, free from agitation, becomes concentrated.
For one whose mind is concentrated, the discernment of wisdom arises.
By means of that, one knows the object as it truly is.
Through the practice of that and through detachment from those respective objects, non-cognitive (asaṃprajñāta) samādhi arises.
Indeed, those nine types of yogins possess mild, middling, or intense means.
Namely: the weak method, the middling method, and the superior method.
Among these, the weak method is threefold: weak urgency, middling urgency, and intense urgency.
Likewise for the middling method, and likewise for the superior method.
Among those, for those with superior means—
those characterized by intense urgency— the [attainment of samādhi] is near.
The attainment of concentration and its fruit come about;
moreover, there is a distinction even from that due to its being mild, moderate, or intense.
[The degrees of intensity are] mild-intense, medium-intense, and supreme-intense.
There is a distinction even from that.

Due to that distinction, for one with mild-intense urgency, the attainment of concentration and its fruit is near; for one with medium-intense urgency, it is nearer; and for one with supreme-intense urgency and supreme means, the attainment of concentration and its fruit is nearest of all.
Is this concentration the very nearest one?
Or, upon its attainment, is there some other means as well, or not?—[it is said:
"Or by devotion to Īśvara" (YS 1.23).
[YS 1.23] Through his devotion and specific aspiration, the Lord is inclined toward him and favors him by mere contemplation.
Even from that mere contemplation, for the yogin, the attainment of samādhi and the fruit of samādhi become most immediate.
Now, who is this so-called Īśvara, distinct from both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*?—
Īśvara is a particular *puruṣa* untouched by afflictions (*kleśa*), actions (*karman*), their fruitions (*vipāka*), or latent dispositions (*āśaya*).
[Yoga Sūtra 1.24] [Yoga Sūtra 1.24]
Ignorance and the other afflictions;
wholesome and unwholesome actions;
and their result, which is maturation.

The latent impressions (*vāsanā*) corresponding to those [actions] are the dispositions (*āśaya*). Although they reside in the mind (*manas*), they are attributed to the *puruṣa*, for he is the experiencer of their fruit.
Just as victory or defeat, though occurring among the warriors, is attributed to the master.
For that person who is untouched by this experience of worldly enjoyment is the Supreme Person, the Lord (Īśvara). [Objection:

But there are many who have attained isolation (kaivalya) and are now liberated souls (kevalins). They too, having severed the three bonds, have attained isolation; so how is the Lord different? [Response: It is true they have attained it, but for the Lord, that connection with bondage has never existed in the past, nor will it ever exist in the future.
Just as for one who has been liberated, a prior limit of bondage is known, it is not so for Īśvara.
Or, just as for one merged in *prakṛti*, a future limit of bondage is conceivable, it is not so for Īśvara.
He, however, is eternally liberated and eternally the Lord.
Is that eternal excellence of Īśvara, which results from his appropriation of preeminent *sattva*, caused by something or is it without cause?
Scripture (*śāstra*) is its cause.
But what is the cause of scripture? It has preeminent *sattva* as its cause.
The relationship between these two—the excellence of scripture and the existence of God—is beginningless.
From this it follows that God is eternally so and eternally liberated. Furthermore, His sovereignty is devoid of both equality and superiority.
That [supreme state] cannot be surpassed by any other form of sovereignty;
for whatever might surpass it would itself be that [very state].
Therefore, he in whom sovereignty has reached its ultimate limit is the Lord (Īśvara).
Nor is there any sovereignty equal to that [of Ishvara].

Why? Because when two equals simultaneously desire the same object—thinking, "Let this be new" and "Let this be old"—if one succeeds, the other's power of will (*prākāmya*) is frustrated, which results in inferiority.
Furthermore, it is impossible for two equals to simultaneously attain the object they have desired.
Because it would be contradictory to the [established] meaning.
Therefore, he alone is the Lord whose sovereignty is devoid of equality and superiority;
and he is a particular kind of spirit (puruṣaviśeṣa).
Furthermore:
"In that state, the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed" (YS 1.25).

This apprehension of the past, future, and present—whether individually or collectively—and of objects beyond the senses, whether small or great, is the seed of omniscience (*sarvajñabīja*). As this seed increases until it reaches a point where there is no further excellence, that [state] is omniscience.
There is a reaching of the ultimate limit for the seed of omniscience because it is subject to degrees of excellence, like any measurable magnitude.
That in which knowledge reaches its ultimate limit is the omniscient one.
And that person is a particular individual.
Furthermore, since inference is exhausted by establishing a mere generality, it is not capable of bringing about the cognition of a particular;
therefore, the cognition of his specific name and other particulars must be sought from scripture (*āgama*).
Even though there is no benefit for himself, his purpose is the benefit of living beings:
"By means of the instruction in knowledge and dharma, I shall uplift transmigrating persons during the kalpa-dissolutions and the great dissolution.
And so it has been said: "The primordial Knower, the Blessed One, the supreme Sage, having presided over a mind of emanation, out of compassion taught the Tantra to Āsuri, who desired to know it."
This very one is the teacher even of the ancients, because he is not limited by time.
For previous teachers are delimited by time;
but he, in whom time does not apply for the purpose of delimitation, is the teacher even of those predecessors.

Just as he was established at the beginning of this creation through the attainment of excellence, so too should he be understood to have been so established at the beginnings of past creations as well.
The Praṇava is its designator;
Īśvara is the designated object of the Praṇava.
Is its status as signifier and signified created by convention, or is it established like the light of a lamp?
The relationship between this signified and its signifier is established;
convention, however, merely indicates the already existing meaning for the sake of the listener.

Just as the relationship between father and son, which exists as it is, is made manifest through convention by saying, "this is his father" and "this is his son," so too in other creations (sargāntara) is convention established in that very same way, depending upon the power of the signifier and the signified.
Because of the permanence of this common understanding, the followers of tradition (āgaminaḥ) maintain that the relationship between word and meaning is eternal.
For the yogi who has understood the relationship between the signifier and the signified,
there is the repetition of that [mantra] and meditation on its meaning.
The repetition of the *praṇava* and the contemplation of the Lord who is denoted by the *praṇava*:
for this yogin who repeats the *praṇava* and contemplates its meaning, the mind becomes one-pointed.
And so it has been said:
"From self-study one should practice yoga; from yoga one should attend to self-study. Through the perfection of both self-study and yoga, the Supreme Self is revealed.
Furthermore, what happens for him?
"Then there is the attainment of the inward-turned consciousness and the absence of obstacles" (Yoga Sūtra 1.29).
[YS 1.29] Those obstacles which consist of disease and so forth do not occur due to devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna).
Furthermore, there arises for him the vision of his own true nature.
Just as the Lord Puruṣa is pure, serene, absolute, and free from afflictions, so too does one attain that Puruṣa who is the witness of the intellect.
Now, what are the obstacles which are the distractions of the mind?
Furthermore, what are they, and how many are there?
Sickness, languor, doubt, heedlessness, laziness, lack of dispassion, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage, and instability— these distractions of the mind are the obstacles.
(YS 1.30) There are nine obstacles which are distractions of the mind.
These [obstacles] arise together with the fluctuations of the mind;
in their absence, the aforementioned fluctuations of the mind do not occur. Disease is a disorder of the humors, the fluids, and the organs.
Styāna is the lack of serviceability of the mind.
Saṃśaya is a cognition that touches upon two alternatives, thinking "it might be thus" or "it might not be thus.
Pramāda is the non-cultivation of the means for achieving meditative concentration.
Laziness is the non-activation of both body and mind due to heaviness.
Non-restraint is the greed of the mind characterized by its attachment to sense objects.
Erroneous vision is inverted cognition.
The state of not having attained the stage (*alabdhabhūmikatva*) is the non-attainment of the stage of meditative concentration (*samādhibhūmi*).

The state of instability (*anavasthitatva*) is the mind’s failure to remain established once that stage has been attained; for if meditative concentration were indeed attained, the mind would remain fixed therein.
These nine distractions of the mind are designated as the impurities of yoga, the adversaries of yoga, and the obstacles to yoga.
Pain, mental distress, trembling of the limbs, and labored breathing and exhaling are concomitants of distraction.
Suffering is internal, external, and celestial.
That by which living beings are struck and strive for its removal is suffering. Mental distress is the agitation of the mind resulting from the frustration of one's desires.
That which causes the limbs to quiver and tremble is "limb-trembling" (*aṅgamejayatva*).
When the breath (*prāṇa*) inhales external air, that is inhalation (*śvāsa*);
when it expels the abdominal air, that is exhalation (*praśvāsa*).
These are the factors that coexist with distraction; they occur in one whose mind is distracted, but they do not occur in one whose mind is concentrated.
Now, since these distractions are the adversaries of concentration, they must be suppressed by those very two means: cultivation and detachment.
In this regard, while concluding the subject matter concerning practice, he says this:
"To prevent that, practice on a single principle" (YS 1.32).
For the purpose of preventing distraction, one should practice a mind that rests upon a single principle (*ekatattva*).

However, for one who holds that the mind consists merely of momentary cognitions restricted to each respective object, every mind would necessarily be one-pointed and there would be no such thing as a distracted mind.

If, on the other hand, this [mind] were withdrawn from all [objects] and concentrated upon a single object, then it would become one-pointed; therefore, [the mind] is not restricted to each respective object.

Even for one who considers the mind to be one-pointed through a stream of similar cognitions, if that one-pointedness is a property of the "stream-mind," then such a stream-mind does not exist as a single entity because of its momentariness.

If, on the other hand, it is a property of each individual cognition within the stream, then every cognition—whether belonging to a stream of similar cognitions or a stream of dissimilar cognitions—is necessarily one-pointed because it is restricted to its own respective object; consequently, a distracted mind would be impossible.
Therefore, the mind is a single entity, directed toward multiple objects, and enduring.

Furthermore, if cognitions were to arise as distinct in nature and unconnected by a single mind, then how could one cognition be the rememberer of what was seen by another cognition? And how could one cognition be the experiencer of the latent deposit of karma accumulated by another cognition?
Even if this were somehow reconciled, it would fall into the logic of the "cow-dung and milk-porridge" analogy.
Furthermore, if the mind were something other [than the self], it would entail the denial of one's own self-experience.

How so? The cognition "I," expressed as "What I saw, that I touch; and what I touched, that I see," presents itself as non-different from the cognizer even when every individual cognition is distinct.

How could this cognition "I," which has a single cognition as its object and is non-dual in nature, subsist upon many minds that are absolutely distinct, unless it rested upon a single, common cognizer?
Moreover, this cognition "I," which is non-dual in nature, is graspable through one's own direct experience (*svānubhava*).
Nor is the majesty of perception (*pratyakṣa*) overridden by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
rather, it is precisely by the power of perception that other means of valid cognition obtain their conventional application in worldly affairs.
Therefore, the mind is both unitary and manifold in its objects, and it is stable.
Regarding that stable mind for which this preparatory purification is taught by the treatise, how is it described?
"The clarification of the mind arises from the cultivation of friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward objects that are happy, suffering, virtuous, and non-virtuous" (Yoga Sūtra 1.33).
In that regard, one should cultivate friendliness toward all living beings who are experiencing happiness;
and compassion toward those who are suffering.
He cultivates sympathetic joy toward those whose nature is meritorious,
and equanimity toward those of non-meritorious conduct.
As he meditates in this way, a pure quality arises within him.
And from that, the mind becomes serene;
being serene and one-pointed, it attains the state of stability.
Or else, [stability is attained] through the expulsion and retention of the breath (prāṇa). [YS 1.34]

[YS 1.34] Vomiting the abdominal air through the nostrils by means of a specific effort is *pracchardana*; its restraint is *prāṇāyāma*. Through these two, or through them, one may achieve steadiness of the mind.
Or, an activity directed toward an object that has arisen serves as a basis for the steadiness of the mind. [YS 1.35]
[YS 1.35] For one who fixes the mind on the tip of the nose, that consciousness of divine fragrance is the manifestation of smell;
on the tip of the tongue, it is the consciousness of taste.
The perception of form occurs in the palate; the perception of touch occurs in the middle of the tongue;
the perception of sound occurs at the root of the tongue. These functions, when arisen, bind the mind to stability, dispel doubt, and serve as gateways to the wisdom of samādhi.

By this, it should be understood that the cognitive activity directed toward the moon, the sun, planets, jewels, lamps, rays of light, and so forth, occurs only when there is an object present. For although the reality of an object is indeed truly existent as it is understood through those respective scriptures, inference, and the instructions of teachers—due to these [authorities'] capacity to convey things as they actually are—nevertheless, as long as even some single part is not cognizable by one's own sense-faculties, the whole remains as if beyond perception; thus, regarding subtle matters such as liberation and the like, it does not produce a firm cognition.
Therefore, for the sake of strengthening scripture, inference, and the instructions of the teacher, some specific object must necessarily be made perceptible.
When one part of the object taught by them has been perceived, everything—even that which concerns subtle objects—up to final liberation (*apavarga*) is accepted with faith.
It is for this very purpose that this mental cultivation (*cittaparikarma*) is prescribed.
When mastery over the indeterminate fluctuations has arisen regarding their objects, one will be capable of bringing each respective object into direct perception.
And this being so, faith, energy, mindfulness, and concentration will follow for him without obstruction.
Or, there is the "joyless" [meditation], which is "luminous" (YS 1.36).
[YS 1.36] "The activity that has arisen serves as a support for the steadiness of the mind"—this phrase carries over.

For one who holds the mind in the lotus of the heart, there arises a cognitive awareness (*buddhi-saṃvit*); for the *sattva* of the intellect is luminous and like space. Through proficiency in remaining steady therein, this activity manifests in various forms, such as the appearances of the light of the sun, moon, planets, and jewels.

Likewise, the mind that has attained the meditative absorption of *asmitā* (I-am-ness) becomes like a great ocean without waves—tranquil, infinite, and consisting of *asmitā* alone. Regarding this, it is said: "Having realized that Self which is subtle as an atom, one perceives it with the simple awareness, 'I am. This twofold manifestation—both the object-possessing (*viṣayavatī*) and the *asmitā*-only state—is called the luminous (*jyotiṣmatī*) activity.
By means of which the mind of the yogi attains a state of stability:
"Or the mind has as its object one who is free from passion" (YS 1.37).
Or, the yogi’s mind, colored by an object that is the mind of one free from passion, attains a state of stability;
or it takes as its object the cognition of dream or sleep.
Or, the yogi’s mind, having as its object either dream-cognition or sleep-cognition and taking on their form, attains a state of stability;
or [it attains stability] through meditation on whatever is desired.
One should meditate upon whatever is desired. Having attained stability therein, one attains the state of stability elsewhere as well.
Its mastery extends from the smallest atom to the greatest magnitude. [YS 1.40]

For one entering into the subtle, the mind attains a state of stability reaching down to the ultimate atom; for one entering into the gross, the mind attains a state of stability reaching up to the ultimate magnitude.
Thus, for one who pursues both these extremes, that non-obstruction which arises is the supreme mastery (*vaśīkāra*).
Through that mastery, the mind of the yogi becomes perfected and no longer requires preparatory refinement (*parikarma*) produced by repeated practice.
Now, as to what the nature and what the object of the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) are for a mind that has attained stability—that is being explained:

"For one whose fluctuations have ceased, there is, as it were, for a noble gem, a meditative attainment (samāpatti) consisting of resting in and being colored by that [object], with respect to the grasper, the grasping, and the graspable" (YS 1.41).
"For one whose fluctuations have ceased" means for one whose cognitive modifications have subsided.
The phrase "like a well-bred gem" is an illustration.

Just as a crystal, through contact with various objects, becomes colored by their respective forms and appears in the form and shape of those objects it rests upon, so too the mind, colored by the object of perception (*grāhya*), becomes absorbed in that object and appears in the very form and nature of the perceived object.
When colored by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), it becomes absorbed in the subtle elements and manifests as the appearance of the essential nature of the subtle elements.
In the same way, colored by a gross object, it becomes absorbed in a gross form and appears as a gross form.
Likewise, colored by the diversity of the universe, it becomes absorbed in the diversity of the universe and appears as the universal form.
This should be understood to apply similarly to the instruments of perception, that is, the sense organs as well.

Colored by the object of perception (*grahaṇālambana*), having attained the state of perception (*grahaṇasamāpanna*), it manifests in the form of the essential nature of perception (*grahaṇasvarūpākāra*).

Likewise, colored by the object of the perceiving person (*grahītṛpuruṣālambana*), having attained the state of the perceiving person (*grahītṛpuruṣasamāpanna*), it manifests in the form of the essential nature of the perceiving person (*grahītṛpuruṣasvarūpākāra*).

Likewise, colored by the object of the liberated person (*muktapuruṣālambana*), having attained the state of the liberated person (*muktapuruṣasamāpanna*), it manifests in the form of the essential nature of the liberated person (*muktapuruṣasvarūpākāra*).

Thus, for the mind—which is like a noble jewel—there is that state of being established in and colored by those [objects], namely the perceiver, the means of perception, and the perceived, which consist of the person (*puruṣa*), the senses, and the elements; this assuming of their form while established in them is called "absorption" (*samāpatti*).
Among these, absorption mixed with the conceptual constructions of words, objects, and knowledge is "with deliberation" (*savitarka*).
(Yogasūtra 1.42)
For example, the word "cow," the object "cow," and the cognition "cow" are perceived as undifferentiated, even though they are distinct.
When analyzed, however, their paths are separate: the properties of sound are one thing, the properties of the object another, and the properties of consciousness yet another.

In that context, when a yogin has attained meditative absorption (*samāpanna*), if the object such as a cow that has ascended into the wisdom of concentration (*samādhi-prajñā*) returns accompanied by the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of word, object, and cognition, that is a mixed attainment and is called "with deliberation" (*savitarka*).

Furthermore, when the memory of linguistic conventions has been purified, and in the wisdom of meditative concentration (samādhi-prajñā) which is devoid of the conceptual constructions of knowledge derived from scripture or inference, the object remains established in its own essential nature alone; it is then delimited solely by the form of that essential nature.
This is the attainment free from discursive thought (nirvitarka-samāpatti).
That is supreme perception (pratyakṣa).
And that is the seed of both scripture and inference;
from it, scripture and inference arise.
Furthermore, that vision does not coexist with the cognition of scripture and inference.
Therefore, the vision of the yogi born from the *nirvitarka* concentration is unmixed with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The definition of this *nirvitarka* attainment is illuminated by the Sūtra:
"When memory is purified, the *nirvitarka* [attainment] is that in which the object alone appears, as if devoid of its own form" (YS 1.43).

[YS 1.43] That wisdom (*prajñā*) which, when purified of the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) consisting of the knowledge derived from verbal convention, hearing, and inference, and being colored by the true nature of the object of perception, abandons as it were its own nature as a perceiving subject and becomes the very nature of the thing alone—as if having assumed the nature of the object itself—is then the *nirvitarka* (non-discursive) attainment.
And thus it has been explained: "The world, whether it be a cow or a jar, consists of a particular accumulation of atoms whose essence is the object, and it is approached by a single cognition."

And that specific configuration, which is a common property inherent in the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), inferred by its manifested effect and brought to manifestation by its own manifestors, appears;
and upon the arising of other properties such as the potsherds, it disappears.
This very property is called the "whole" (*avayavin*).
It is that which is unitary, great, subtle, tangible, characterized by activity, and impermanent—by means of such a whole (*avayavin*) that worldly transactions are conducted.

For one, however, for whom that particular accumulation is without a real substrate, the cause is subtle and unperceivable; since there is no whole for that non-conceptual [cognition], it is a false cognition not established in its true form. Thus, it follows that almost all cognition would be false.
And in that case, would even right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) exist, given the absence of an object?
Whatever is perceived is traditionally taught to be a whole (*avayavin*).
Therefore, there exists a whole which, having attained the status of being large and so forth, becomes the object of the non-discursive (*nirvitarkā*) meditative attainment.
By this very same [definition], the subtle-objected [samādhis] with deliberation (*savicārā*) and without deliberation (*nirvicārā*) are explained.

Among those, the attainment (*samāpatti*) which occurs regarding the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*)— in which the properties (*dharma*) are manifested and which are delimited by the experience of place, time, and cause— is called "with deliberation."

In that state as well, the subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*), which is to be grasped by a single cognition and is distinguished by the aforementioned qualities, stands as the object (*ālambana*) for the wisdom (*prajñā*) of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, that meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) which occurs with respect to all things—whether past, present, or unpredicable—which are undifferentiated, which follow after all phenomena, and whose nature consists of all phenomena, is called "without deliberation" (*nirvicārā*).
For the subtle element, being of such a nature, when it becomes the object in its very own form, colors the nature of the wisdom of meditative concentration accordingly.
And when wisdom (*prajñā*) becomes, as it were, empty of its own nature and consists of the object alone, it is then called "beyond reflection" (*nirvicārā*).

Among these, that which has gross objects as its domain is "with deliberation" (*savitarkā*) and "without deliberation" (*nirvitarkā*); that which has subtle objects as its domain is "with reflection" (*savicārā*) and "without reflection" (*nirvicārā*).
Thus, by this very [state of] being "without deliberation," the abandonment of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) for both [types of concentration] is explained.
And the state of having subtle objects culminates in the unmanifest (aliṅga) [YS 1.45].
For an earthly atom, the subtle object is the subtle element of odor (gandhatanmātra).
From the watery [element] comes the subtle element of taste;
from the fiery [element], the subtle element of form;
from the airy [element], the subtle element of touch.

The subtle element of sound belongs to space. Of these [subtle elements], the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is the cause; for this [ego-sense] as well, the subtle object is the "merely indicative" (liṅgamātra).
Even for the mere *liṅga*, the unmanifest (*aliṅga*) is the subtle object. And there is nothing subtler than the unmanifest.
[Objection: But surely the Puruṣa is subtle? [Reply: True.
Just as the subtlety of the unmanifest (aliṅga) is superior to that of the manifest (liṅga), it is not so with the Puruṣa.
Rather, the Puruṣa is not the material cause (anvayikāraṇa) of the manifest, though he is its efficient cause (hetu).
Therefore, the subtlety in the Pradhāna is explained as being unsurpassed.
"These indeed are the seeded concentration" (YS 1.46).
Since those four attainments have external objects as their seeds, the concentration is also "seeded."

In that regard, concentration is enumerated as fourfold: with deliberation (*savitarka*) and without deliberation (*nirvitarka*) regarding gross objects, and with reflection (*savicāra*) and without reflection (*nirvicāra*) regarding subtle objects.
When there is mastery over the state of being without reflection, there is internal clarity (*adhyātmaprasāda*).

The clarity (*vaiśāradya*) of the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*), whose nature is luminosity and from which the impurities of the veil of defilement have been removed, is its clear, steady flow when it is not overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*.

When this clarity of the *nirvicāra* (non-discursive) samādhi arises, then for the yogin there occurs an internal serenity (*adhyātmaprasāda*), a vivid light of wisdom (*prajñāloka*) whose object is the true reality (*bhūtārtha*), which does not follow a temporal sequence.

Thus it has been said: "Having ascended to the clarity of wisdom, the wise man, beyond grief, looks upon all grieving people as one standing on a mountain peak looks down upon those standing on the ground."
Having ascended the palace of wisdom, the wise man, beyond grief, looks down upon grieving people;
like one standing on a mountain peak looking at those on the ground, he beholds all.
Therein, wisdom is that which bears truth. [Yoga Sūtra 1.48]
[YS 1.48] The wisdom that arises for one whose mind is concentrated upon that [object] receives the designation "truth-bearing" (*ṛtambharā*).
This term is literal in meaning, for it bears only the truth; there is not even a trace of erroneous cognition present therein.
And so it has been said:
"By means of scripture, by inference, and by the savor of the practice of meditation—cultivating wisdom in these three ways—one attains the supreme yoga. [Namely:
by means of scripture, by inference, and by the savor of the practice of meditation.
By cultivating wisdom in three ways, one attains the supreme yoga.
Furthermore, that [wisdom] has a different object from the wisdoms derived from hearing and inference, because it pertains to specific particulars. [YS 1.49]
[YS 1.49] Śruta is the knowledge derived from scripture; it has only the universal as its object.
For a particular cannot be expressed by means of scripture. Why? Because a word is not conventionally established for a particular.
Likewise, inference has only the universal as its object.
It has been stated that where there is attainment, there is movement; where there is non-attainment, there is no movement.
And by means of inference, the conclusion is reached through the universal.
Therefore, there is no particularity whatsoever that falls within the scope of scripture or inference.
Nor is there any apprehension of this subtle, concealed, or remote object by means of worldly perception.

And since this particularity cannot be non-existent if it lacks a means of valid cognition, that particularity—whether pertaining to the subtle elements or to the *puruṣa*—is to be grasped solely by the wisdom born of meditative concentration (*samādhi-prajñā*).
Therefore, that wisdom has a different object from the wisdoms derived from scripture and inference, because it pertains to specific particulars.
Upon the attainment of the wisdom of samādhi, a new and ever-new impression produced by that wisdom arises for the yogin—
*the impression born therefrom obstructs other impressions* (Yoga Sūtra 1.50).
The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the wisdom of *samādhi* sublates the substrate of latent impressions arising from the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*).
Because the latent impressions of emergence are suppressed, the cognitions (*pratyaya*) produced from them do not arise.
When conditions cease, concentration is established.
From that arises wisdom born of concentration; from that arise formations produced by wisdom. Thus, a new and ever-new store of formations is generated.
And from that comes wisdom, and from that come formations.
How could this excellence of formative forces (*saṃskārātiśaya*) not leave the mind with a further task?
Those formative forces produced by wisdom do not render the mind distinguished by a further task, because they are the cause for the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Indeed, they cause the mind to cease from its own activity.
For the activity of the mind culminates in cognition.
And what happens to it?
"When that too ceases, because of the cessation of everything, there is seedless samādhi" (YS 1.51).
[YS 1.51] It is not only an obstacle to the wisdom of samādhi, but it also becomes an impediment to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by that wisdom.
Why? Because the latent impression born of cessation (*nirodha*) subverts the latent impressions born of samādhi.

The existence of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the mind in the state of cessation (*nirodha*) is to be inferred from the experience of the sequence of time during the duration of that cessation.

When the mind, together with the latent impressions conducive to liberation (*kaivalyabhāgīya*) arising from both the emergent and the suppressive concentrations (*samādhi*), dissolves into its own primordial nature (*prakṛti*),
those latent impressions become antagonistic to the mind's functional capacity (*adhikāra*) and no longer serve as causes for its continued existence.

Because the mind, having completed its office, ceases together with the latent impressions conducive to isolation (*kaivalya*), when that [mind] has ceased, the *puruṣa* is established in its own nature alone; therefore, it is called pure, isolated, and liberated.

Thus ends the first chapter, the Samādhi-pāda, in the illustrious Pātañjala Yoga-śāstra, the Exposition of Sāṃkhya, the commentary by the venerable Vyāsa. [The Second Chapter: The Means of Attainment].
The yoga of one whose mind is concentrated has been taught.
Now this is undertaken: how might one whose mind is emergent also be joined with yoga?
"Austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord constitute the yoga of action" (YS 2.1).
[YS 2.1] Yoga is not accomplished for one who lacks austerity (*tapas*).

Since impurity— which is variegated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of beginningless karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) and which presents a web of sense objects— does not undergo dissolution without austerity, austerity is therefore undertaken.
And one considers that this practice of mental clarity should be cultivated as long as it does not cause affliction.
Recitation (*svādhyāya*) is the chanting of purificatory mantras such as the *praṇava*, or the study of the scriptures on liberation.
Devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) is the dedication of all actions to the Supreme Teacher, or the renunciation of their fruits.
For that indeed is the yoga of action (kriyāyoga)—
for the purpose of cultivating meditative absorption (samādhi) and for the purpose of attenuating the afflictions (kleśa). [YS 2.2] [YS 2.2]
For when that [practice] is cultivated, it develops meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and attenuates the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Having attenuated the afflictions, it will render them incapable of further production, like seeds burnt by the fire of discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*).

Because they have been attenuated, the subtle wisdom—the manifestation of the mere distinction between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, untouched by the afflictions—having fulfilled its purpose, will be fit for re-absorption (*pratiprasava*).
Now, what are the afflictions and how many are there?— ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the afflictions (YS 2.3).
The "afflictions" (kleśa) mean the five types of misconceptions (viparyaya).

When they are active, they strengthen the authority of the guṇas, establish their transformation, raise up the stream of cause and effect, and—acting as mutual supports—they bring about the ripening of karma (karmavipāka). Ignorance (avidyā) is the field for the others—those that are dormant, attenuated, interrupted, or active. (Yogasūtra 2.4)
[YS 2.4] Here, ignorance is the field, the ground of production, for the four types of fluctuations beginning with egoism— namely, those that are dormant, attenuated, interrupted,
and active. Among these, what is dormancy?
The transition into the state of a seed consists in the subsistence of mere potencies within the mind. Its awakening is its manifestation toward an object.

For one who possesses discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) and whose seeds of affliction have been burnt, this [awakening] does not occur again even when an object is present; for how can there be the sprouting of a burnt seed?
Therefore, one whose afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted is called "virtuous" (*kuśala*) and "in his final body.
In that very state, the fifth stage of the afflictions has its seeds burnt away, and not elsewhere.

Since the potency of the seeds of the existing afflictions has been burnt at that time, even when an object is present before them, their awakening does not occur; thus, the dormant state and the non-sprouting of burnt seeds have been described.
"Attenuation" is said as follows: the afflictions, being struck down by the cultivation of their antidotes, become attenuated.
Likewise, they are "interrupted" because they arise again and again in various forms after having been repeatedly severed.
How so? Because at the time of passion, anger is not observed.
For at the time of passion, anger does not manifest.
Furthermore, when passion is observed in one instance, it is not absent in other objects.

It is not the case that when Caitra is impassioned toward one woman, he is consequently dispassionate toward other women; rather, in that case, passion has attained its functional state (*labdhavṛtti*), whereas in other cases, it will attain its functional state in the future (*bhaviṣyadvṛtti*).
For at that time, it is either dormant, attenuated, or interrupted.
That which has attained its functional state with respect to an object is called "gross.
All of these, without exception, do not transcend the status of being objects for the afflictions (*kleśa*).
What, then, is meant by a "dormant," "subtle," or "active" affliction? It is said: this is indeed true; however, these qualities of being dormant and so forth apply only to specific [afflictions].
Just as they have ceased through the cultivation of their antidotes, so too are they manifested by the application of their own manifesting conditions.
All these afflictions are merely varieties of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Why? Because ignorance alone pervades all [afflictions].

Whatever object is constructed by ignorance, it is precisely therein that the afflictions lie dormant; they are perceived at the time of the conditions for error, and as ignorance wanes, they wane along with it.
In this regard, the essential nature of ignorance is stated:
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the perception of the eternal, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in that which is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self.
[YS 2.5] Regarding the impermanent effect, it is the perception of the eternal.
For example: "The earth is eternal; the sky with its moon and stars is eternal; the dwellers of heaven are immortal.
Yet, regarding this body which is impure and supremely loathsome, it is said:
"Because of its origin, its seed, its support, its discharge, and its end, and because it must be cleansed, the wise indeed know the body to be impure."
Because of its location, its seed, its support, its outflow, and its end,
as well as because it requires purification, the wise indeed know the body to be impure.

Thus, the perception of purity in the impure is observed. [One thinks: "This lovely girl is like a fresh crescent moon; she seems as if fashioned from the very limbs of honey and nectar, or as if she has emerged after piercing through the moon. With eyes as long as the petals of a blue lotus, she seems to comfort the world of the living with her glances full of amorous gestures. What connection can there be between these things?
And yet, such a cognition of purity arises regarding the impure.
By this, the notion of merit regarding that which is non-meritorious, as well as the notion of benefit regarding that which is harmful, has been explained.

Likewise, he will state the perception of pleasure within suffering: "To the discerning person, all is indeed suffering because of the sufferings of transformation, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict between the functions of the *guṇas*.
In that context, the perception of pleasure is ignorance (*avidyā*).

Likewise, there is the manifestation of the self (*ātma-khyāti*) in that which is not the self: in external instruments, whether sentient or insentient; or in the body, which is the locus of experience; or in the mind, which is an instrument of the *puruṣa*. Thus it has been said here: "Having perceived a manifest or unmanifest entity as the self, one rejoices in its prosperity, thinking it to be the prosperity of the self, and grieves over its misfortune, thinking it to be the misfortune of the self; all such a person is unawakened."
This consists of four lines: "Ignorance is the root of this continuum of afflictions and of the latent deposit of karma together with its maturation.
And the reality of that [ignorance] should be understood to be like [the expressions] "non-friend" or "non-cow-track.
Just as "non-friend" is neither the absence of a friend nor merely a friend, but rather an adversary who is the opposite of a friend; so too is ignorance.

Just as the term *agoṣpada* refers neither to the absence of a cow’s footprint nor merely to a cow’s footprint, but rather to a distinct entity—a specific location different from those two—so too, *avidyā* (ignorance) is neither valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor the absence of valid cognition; rather, ignorance is another form of knowledge that is the opposite of *vidyā* (true knowledge).
This is similar to the notion of *asmitā* (egoism), which is the apparent identity between the power of seeing (*dṛk-śakti*) and the power of the seen (*darśana-śakti*).

[YS 2.6] The *puruṣa* is the power of seeing; the intellect (*buddhi*) is the power of seeing. The affliction called *asmitā* (I-am-ness) is said to be like the attainment of a single nature between these two. When there is, as it were, a state of non-differentiation between the power of the enjoyer and the power of the object of enjoyment—which are absolutely distinct and absolutely unmixed—experience (*bhoga*) is possible.
But upon the attainment of their own true nature (*svarūpa*), those two exist in isolation alone; how, then, could there be experience?

Thus it has been said: "Not seeing the Puruṣa as distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*) by virtue of its form, character, knowledge, and so forth, one might, through delusion, form the notion of self (*ātmabuddhi*) with respect to that [intellect]. [And:
"Attachment is that which rests upon pleasure" (YS 2.7).
[YS 2.7] For one who has experienced pleasure, that greed, thirst, or lust which arises toward pleasure or its means, preceded by the recollection of that pleasure, is attachment (*rāga*).
Aversion (*dveṣa*) is that which lies latent within suffering. [YS 2.8]
[YS 2.8] Hatred (dveṣa) is that aversion, resentment, desire to strike, or anger directed toward suffering or its causes, preceded by the recollection of suffering in one who has experienced it.
[YS 2.9] Clinging to life (abhiniveśa) is a natural flow that is firmly rooted even in the wise man.
[YS 2.9] This self-wish is eternal for every living being: "May I not cease to be; may I continue to exist.
And this self-wish does not arise in one who has not experienced the nature of death.
And by this, the experience of a previous birth is recognized.

This very clinging (*abhiniveśa*), which is a spontaneous affliction (*kleśa*), is the fear of death—an instance of the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*)—which is impossible to account for through perception, inference, or scripture even in a worm immediately upon its birth; it leads one to infer the suffering of death experienced in a previous life.
Just as this affliction is seen among those who are utterly ignorant, so too is it firmly rooted even in the wise person who understands the prior and subsequent limits of existence.
Why? Because this latent impression (*vāsanā*) arises from the experience of the suffering of death for both of them, whether their state be wholesome or unwholesome.
These subtle impressions are to be abandoned through reabsorption (*pratiprasava*).
(Yogasūtra 2.10)
Those five afflictions, resembling burnt seeds, set along with that very mind when the mind has ceased its function for the practitioner;
however, for those who remain, having entered the state of seeds—their fluctuations are to be abandoned by meditative absorption (dhyāna). [Yoga Sūtra 2.11]

[YS 2.11] Those gross manifestations of the afflictions (kleśa) which have been attenuated by the practice of action-yoga (kriyāyoga) must be abandoned through higher discernment (prasaṃkhyāna), that is, through meditative absorption (dhyāna), until they are rendered subtle, like seeds that have been burnt.

Just as the gross dirt on clothes is shaken off first, while the fine residue is removed later with effort and skillful means, so too the gross manifestations of the afflictions have weak counteragents, whereas the subtle ones require powerful counteragents.
The latent deposit of karma has its root in the afflictions; it is to be experienced in this life or in future lives.
Among these, the latent deposit of meritorious and non-meritorious karma arises from desire, greed, delusion, and anger.
It is both to be experienced in the present life and to be experienced in a future life.

Among these, that which is accomplished through intense fervor by means of mantras, austerities, and meditative concentrations, or which is perfected through the propitiation of the Lord, the gods, the great seers, and those of great majesty—that accumulation of meritorious karma ripens immediately.

Likewise, when harm is repeatedly inflicted with intense affliction upon those who are terrified, diseased, or miserable, or upon those who have placed their trust in one, or upon those of great majesty or ascetics—that accumulation of sinful karma also ripens immediately.

Just as the youth Nandīśvara, having abandoned his human transformation, was transformed into a deity, so too Nahuṣa, the Indra of the gods, having abandoned his own transformation, was transformed into an animal. In that regard, for those in the hells, there is no latent potential of karma (*karmāśaya*) to be experienced in the present life.
Even for those whose afflictions have been destroyed, there is no latent deposit of karma to be experienced in a future birth;
for when the root exists, its fruition consists of birth, lifespan, and experience.
When the afflictions (*kleśa*) exist, the latent disposition of karma (*karmāśaya*) becomes capable of producing its fruition (*vipāka*), but not when the root of the afflictions has been severed.

Just as rice grains covered by husks are capable of sprouting provided their seed-nature has not been burnt, whereas those from which the husks have been removed or whose seed-nature is burnt are not, so too the latent disposition of karma covered by afflictions leads to the sprouting of fruition, but not when the afflictions have been removed, nor when the seed-nature of the afflictions has been burnt away by discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*).
And that fruition is threefold: birth, lifespan, and experience.
In this regard, the following is investigated: Is a single action the cause of a single birth, or does a single action project multiple births?
This is the second investigation: Do multiple actions bring about multiple births, or do multiple actions bring about a single birth?
First of all, a single action is not the cause of a single birth.

Why? Because, since there would be no fixed order for the ripening of the fruits of the countless remaining karmas accumulated since beginningless time as well as of present karma, a lack of confidence among people would result, which is undesirable.
Furthermore, a single karma cannot be the cause of multiple births.
Why? Because if each individual karma among many were the cause of multiple births, it would follow that there would be no time for the ripening of the remaining karma, which is also undesirable.
Nor is multiple karma the cause of a single birth.
Why? Because that [single] birth cannot occur simultaneously; it must therefore be said to occur only in succession. And in that case, the aforementioned defect persists.

Therefore, the diverse accumulation of latent impressions (*karmāśaya*) consisting of meritorious and non-meritorious actions, performed during the interval between birth and death, existing in the relationship of primary and secondary factors, becomes manifest at the time of death; having brought about death through a single impulse, it coalesces and produces only one birth.
That birth, by means of that very same karma, acquires its lifespan;
and within that lifespan, experience is accomplished by that very same karma.

This latent deposit of karma (karmāśaya) is designated as having a threefold fruition (trivipāka) because it is the cause of birth, lifespan, and experience. Therefore, it is said to belong to a single existence (ekabhavika).

However, that which is to be experienced in the present life (dṛṣṭajanmavedanīya) initiates either a single fruition, being the cause of experience alone—as in the case of Nandīśvara—or it initiates two fruitions, being the cause of both lifespan and experience—as in the case of Nahuṣa.

However, by these latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—produced through the experience of the maturation of afflictions and karma—this mind has been stupefied since beginningless time and made variegated, as if spread out on all sides like a fish-net with knots; these are the latent impressions preceded by many births.
As for this store of karma (*karmāśaya*), it is said to belong to a single birth.
Those formative forces (*saṃskāra*) which are the causes of memory are the latent impressions, and they are beginningless in time.
That store of karma which pertains to a single existence is both of determinate fruition and of indeterminate fruition.

Among these, this rule applies only to that which is to be experienced in the present life and has determinate fruition, but not to that which is to be experienced in a future life and has indeterminate fruition. Why?

Because for that which is to be experienced in a future life and has indeterminate fruition, there are three possible courses: its destruction before it has ripened; its absorption into a dominant karma; or its long-term persistence, being suppressed by a dominant karma of determinate fruition.

In that regard, the destruction of what has been done but not yet ripened is as follows: just as by the arising of white (meritorious) karma, there is the destruction of black (non-meritorious) karma right here in this very life.

As it is said: "Two types of karma indeed must be known; the single heap of the evil-doer's [karma] destroys [the other] for the one who performs merit. Therefore, you should desire to perform well-done deeds; for in this very world, the wise declare your karma. This refers to the entry into the primary karma.

As it has been said: "There may be a slight intermixture [of karma] that is remediable and tolerable; it is not sufficient to diminish the merit of one who is skilled. Why? Because I possess much other merit, into which this [intermixture] has entered as a mere addition; even in heaven, it will cause only a slight diminution.
Or, there is the long-term persistence of karma that is suppressed by karma whose ripening is certain and predominant.

How so? It has been stated that death is the manifesting cause specifically for karma that is to be experienced in a future life (*adṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*) and whose fruition is fixed (*niyatavipāka*). However, it is not [the manifesting cause] for karma that is to be experienced in a future life but whose fruition is unfixed (*aniyatavipāka*).

As for that karma which is to be experienced in a future life and is of unfixed fruition, it may perish, or it may enter into a state of latency (*āvāpa*), or it may remain suppressed for a long time—until a corresponding manifesting condition brings its fruition toward manifestation.
Because the specific place, time, and cause of that very fruition cannot be determined, this course of karma is manifold and difficult to discern.
Furthermore, the general rule is not set aside by its exceptions; thus, the *karmāśaya* (latent deposit of karma) pertaining to a single birth is acknowledged.
These [fruitions] have joy and suffering as their results, because they have merit and demerit as their causes. [YS 2.14]
[YS 2.14] These—birth, lifespan, and experience—are caused by merit and have happiness as their fruit; they are caused by demerit and have suffering as their fruit.
And just as this suffering is of a contrary nature, so too, even at the time of sensual pleasure, there exists for the yogin a suffering that is of a contrary nature.
How is this established?

"Because of the sufferings of change, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict among the functions of the *guṇas*, everything is indeed suffering for the discerning person" (Yogasūtra 2.15).

Since this experience of pleasure for everyone is permeated by passion (*rāga*) and depends upon means that are either conscious or unconscious, there exists therein a latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) born of passion.
Likewise, one hates the instruments of suffering and becomes deluded; thus, there also exists a latent deposit of karma produced by hatred (*dveṣa*) and delusion (*moha*).
And so it has been said: "Since enjoyment is not possible without harming living beings, there also exists a bodily latent deposit of karma produced by violence (*hiṃsā*)."
And it has been stated that sensual pleasure is ignorance (*avidyā*).
That which is the subsiding of the thirst of the sense faculties for enjoyments is happiness;
that which is the non-subsidence [of that thirst] due to greed is suffering.
Nor is it possible to achieve dispassion toward the sense organs through the repeated practice of enjoyment.
Why? Because, following the repeated practice of enjoyment, passions increase as well as the acuity of the sense organs.
Therefore, the repeated practice of enjoyment is not the means for attaining happiness.
Indeed, he who, seeking pleasure and saturated with sense objects, is submerged in the great mire of suffering, is like one bitten by a venomous snake while fearing only the poison of a scorpion.
This is what is called the "suffering of change" (*pariṇāmaduḥkhatā*); it is adverse even during a state of pleasure and afflicts only the yogi.

Now, what is the "suffering of pain" (*tāpaduḥkhatā*)? It is the experience of pain, permeated by hatred, which depends upon means that are either conscious or unconscious; therein lies the latent deposit of karma born of hatred.

Seeking the means of happiness, one moves through body, speech, and mind; thereafter, by benefiting or harming others, one accumulates merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) through those acts of favoring or afflicting others.
That latent deposit of karma arises from greed and delusion; this is called the suffering of pain (*tāpa-duḥkhatā*).

What, then, is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)? It is that from the experience of pleasure there arises a latent deposit of the formation of pleasure, and from the experience of pain there likewise arises a latent deposit of the formation of pain.
Thus, while the fruition of karma—whether pleasure or pain—is being experienced, there is again an accumulation of karmic latencies (*karmāśaya*).

In this way, this beginningless stream of suffering, having spread forth, causes distress only to the yogi because its nature is contrary [to his state]. Why? Because "the wise man is like the eye-ball."

Just as a thread of wool placed in the eye causes pain through touch, but not so on other parts of the body, even so these sufferings afflict only the yogi who is like the eye, and not the other practitioner.

But for the other [the ordinary person], suffering brought about by his own karma follows him as he repeatedly discards what has been acquired and acquires what has been discarded; pierced on all sides by mental fluctuations variegated by beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—as if permeated by ignorance—he pursues the notions of "I" and "mine" which are to be abandoned. Thus, as each new birth occurs, the threefold torments (*tāpa*) caused by external, internal, and both types of factors overwhelm him. Seeing himself and the multitude of beings thus swept away by this beginningless stream of suffering, the yogi takes refuge in right vision (*samyagdarśana*), the cause of the destruction of all suffering.
And because of the conflict between the functions of the *guṇas*, everything is indeed suffering for the discerning person.

The qualities (*guṇas*) of the intellect—having the forms of illumination, activity, and inertia—become dependent upon one another's assistance and produce a cognition that consists of all three *guṇas*, whether it be peaceful, terrible, or deluded.
Furthermore, since the function of the *guṇas* is mobile, the mind is said to be subject to rapid transformation.
The specific intensities of form and the specific intensities of function are mutually contradictory, whereas the general qualities (sāmānyas) operate together with those intensities.

Thus, these qualities (guṇas), by depending upon one another, produce the notions of pleasure, pain, and delusion; consequently, all of them take on every form. However, their distinction is determined by the relationship of primary and secondary importance among them.
Therefore, for the discerning person, everything is indeed nothing but pain.

Thus, ignorance is the seed of the origin of this great mass of suffering, and right vision is its cause of cessation. This is analogous to the fourfold arrangement of medical science: disease, the cause of disease, health, and medicine.
In this way, this treatise also consists of four sections:
namely, cyclic existence, the cause of cyclic existence, liberation, and the means to liberation.
Among these, cyclic existence, which abounds in suffering, is that which is to be abandoned.
The conjunction of primary matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa) is the cause of that which is to be abandoned.
The absolute cessation of this conjunction is abandonment. The means to abandonment is right vision (samyagdarśana).

In this regard, the essential nature of the agent cannot be something to be abandoned or something to be accepted; for if it were abandoned, it would entail the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*), and if it were accepted, it would entail the doctrine of causality (*hetuvāda*).
If both are rejected, it entails the doctrine of eternalism (*śāśvatavāda*); this is right vision (*samyagdarśana*).
This very scripture is thus designated as "the fourfold array" (*caturvyūha*).
"Future suffering is to be abandoned" (YS 2.16).
Suffering that has passed is already exhausted through experience and does not belong to the category of what is to be abandoned.
And that which is present in its own moment is already mounted upon experience; therefore, it does not become something to be abandoned in another moment.
Consequently, only that future suffering—which is like an eye-ball—afflicts the yogin, and not the other perceiver;
only that [suffering] becomes something to be abandoned.
Therefore, that which is said to be what is to be abandoned is precisely its cause that is specified:
"The conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of what is to be abandoned" (YS 2.17).
The Puruṣa is the seer and the experiencer of the intellect (buddhi). All objects (dharmas) are the seen, mounted upon the sattva of the intellect.

This very "seen," which is like a magnet, becomes the property of the Puruṣa—the master whose nature is seeing—merely by its proximity, since it has become the object of the experience of that action.
Although it has acquired its own nature through another form and is independent, it is dependent because it exists for the sake of another.
The beginningless conjunction of those two—the powers of seeing and being seen—which is produced by objects, is the cause of what is to be abandoned; that is to say, it is the cause of suffering.
And so it has been said: "By abandoning the cause of that conjunction, there may be this ultimate remedy for suffering."

Why? Because one perceives a remedy for that cause of suffering which is to be avoided. For example: the foot-sole is the object to be pierced; the thorn is the piercer; and the avoidance consists in not placing the foot upon the thorn, or placing it while shielded by a sandal. He who knows these three things in the world and initiates a remedy therein does not experience the suffering born of piercing.
Why? Because of the efficacy of perceiving this triad.
Here too, it is *sattva* alone that is the object of affliction by the heating *rajas*.

Why? Because the action of heating resides in its object; the action of heating occurs in the object, which is *sattva*, and not in the *kṣetrajña*, who is unchanging and inactive, since his objective field has already been shown [to be external].
But when *sattva* is being afflicted, the *puruṣa* also suffers along with it, conforming to its form.
