The nature of the object of perception is stated: "The object of perception consists of the elements and the sense organs; its nature is illumination, activity, and inertia; it exists for the purpose of experience and liberation" (YS 2.18).
Sattva is characterized by luminosity;
rajas is characterized by activity; and tamas is characterized by inertia.

These *guṇas* have their distinctions colored by one another; they are subject to transformation, possessing the properties of conjunction and disjunction; they acquire their forms through mutual dependence; and although they stand in the relation of primary and subordinate to one another, their powers remain undivided. They follow the differentiation of powers that are both homogeneous and heterogeneous; they manifest their presence at the time of the *pradhāna*; and even while being subordinate, their existence is inferred through their mere activity within the *pradhāna*. Their capacity is impelled by the duty to accomplish the purpose of the *puruṣa*; they assist by their mere proximity, like magnets; and following the activity of whichever one among them is predominant, they become denotable by the term *pradhāna*, even without a conscious intention.
This is called the "visible" (dṛśya).
This very [unmanifest], consisting of the elements and the senses, transforms into the state of the elements—earth and so forth—in both subtle and gross forms;
likewise, it transforms into the state of the senses—the ear and so forth—in both subtle and gross forms.

But that [manifestation] does not proceed without a purpose; rather, it proceeds by taking a purpose upon itself. For that object of perception exists for the sake of experience and liberation for the Puruṣa.

In this regard, experience (*bhoga*) consists in the ascertainment of the nature of the qualities (*guṇa*), whether desirable or undesirable, which has reached a state of non-discrimination; liberation (*apavarga*) consists in the ascertainment of the true nature of the experiencer.
Apart from these two, there is no other manifestation.

And so it has been said: "Indeed, when all objects are presented—whether they have come into being or not—to the fourth principle, which is of a different and non-different nature from the three qualities acting as agents and the Puruṣa who is a non-agent, and which observes them as a witness to their activity, it suspects that there may be something else beyond what is seen.
How then can these two—experience and liberation, which are produced by the intellect and reside only in the intellect—be attributed to the Puruṣa?

Just as victory or defeat, though occurring among the warriors, is attributed to the master because he is the enjoyer of its fruit, so too bondage and liberation, though occurring in the intellect (*buddhi*) alone, are attributed to the *puruṣa*, for he is the enjoyer of their fruit.
Bondage is the intellect’s failure to complete the purpose of the *puruṣa*; liberation is the fulfillment of that purpose.

By this it is shown that apprehension, retention, reasoning, rejection, knowledge of reality, and attachment—though occurring in the intellect—are superimposed upon the *puruṣa* as having real existence.
For he is the enjoyer of its fruit.
This is now commenced for the purpose of determining the specific distinctions in the nature of the perceivable *guṇas*:
"The stages of the *guṇas* are the particularized (*viśeṣa*), the unparticularized (*aviśeṣa*), the mere-indicative (*liṅgamātra*), and the non-indicative (*aliṅga*) [YS 2.19]."
[YS 2.19] Among these, ether, air, fire, water, and earth are the specific manifestations (*viśeṣa*) of the non-specific subtle elements (*aviśeṣa*) of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

Likewise, the sense organs of cognition—ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose; the organs of action—speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; and the eleventh, the mind, which pertains to all objects—these are the specific manifestations of the non-specific ego-sense (*asmitā*).
This sixteenfold specific transformation of the *guṇas* consists of six non-specific [evolutes]. They are as follows:

the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*), the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*), the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*), and the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*). These five non-specific evolutes—sound and the rest—are characterized respectively by one, two, three, four, and five attributes. The sixth non-specific evolute is the subtle principle of "I-am-ness" (*asmitā-mātra*).
These are the six non-specific transformations of the Great Self, which consists of pure existence (*sattāmātra*).

That Great Principle (*mahattattva*), the mere sign (*liṅgamātra*), which exists beyond the ultimate specificities—abiding within that Great Self consisting of pure existence, these [evolutes] reach the culmination of their growth.

And when they are being reabsorbed, abiding in that very same Great Self consisting of pure existence, they return to that which is neither existence nor non-existence, neither being nor non-being, neither existent nor non-existent—the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), the Signless (*aliṅga*), the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*).

This transformation of theirs which consists of the *liṅga* (the manifest) is called "existence," while the transformation that is beyond the *liṅga* (the unmanifest) is called "neither existence nor non-existence.
In the state of the unmanifest (*aliṅga*), the purpose of the *puruṣa* is not the cause; that is, at the beginning of the unmanifest state, the purpose of the *puruṣa* does not function as a cause.
Thus, the purpose of the *puruṣa* does not serve as the cause for that [unmanifest] state.
That which does not perform a purpose for the person (puruṣārtha) is designated as "eternal" (nitya).

However, at the beginning of the three specific states, the purpose of the person becomes the cause; and since that purpose is the motive, the occasion, and the cause, it is designated as "non-eternal" (anitya).
The *guṇas*, however, which follow all *dharmas*, neither perish nor are they produced.

It is only through the individuals (*vyaktis*), which possess the passing away and arrival of the past and future and are themselves permeated by the *guṇas*, that the *guṇas* appear as if they possessed the properties of arising and perishing.
Just as it is said, "Devadatta is becoming poor."
Why is this? Because it is said, "his cows die," and his poverty results precisely from the death of the cows, not from the loss of his own essential nature; such is the same resolution.
The *aliṅga* (the unmanifest) is proximate to the *liṅgamātra* (the mere manifest); there, that which is conjoined with it is distinguished through the transcendence of the sequence.
Likewise, the six *aviśeṣas* (non-specifics), being conjoined within the *liṅgamātra*, are distinguished according to the fixed order of transformation.
Likewise, within those *viśeṣas*, the elements (*bhūtas*) and the sense organs (*indriyas*), which are intermingled, are distinguished.
And as was stated previously:
since there is no other principle beyond the *viśeṣas*, the *viśeṣas* do not undergo transformation into another principle.
However, their transformations of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*) and of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*) will be explained later.

The object of perception (*dṛśya*) has now been explained; next, this [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of determining the true nature of the perceiver (*draṣṭṛ*): "The seer is pure consciousness alone (*dṛśimātra*); though pure, it beholds the mental modifications (*pratyaya-anupaśya*)" (Yogasūtra 2.20).
"Pure seeing" (dṛśimātra) means the power of vision itself, untouched by any qualifications.
That Puruṣa is the perceiver of the intellect.
It is neither identical with the intellect (*buddhi*) nor entirely different from it.
First of all, it is not identical; why?
Because its objects are both known and unknown, whereas the intellect is subject to transformation (*pariṇāminī*).
And its object—be it a cow or a jar—is both known and unknown, which demonstrates its state of transformation (*pariṇāmitva*).

However, the fact that the subject (*puruṣa*) has an object that is always known illuminates his non-transformative nature (*apariṇāmitva*). Why? Because it is impossible for the intellect (*buddhi*) to be both the subject’s object and [simultaneously] unperceived and perceived; thus, it is established that the subject has an object that is always known, and from that follows his non-transformative nature.
Furthermore, the intellect (*buddhi*) exists for the sake of another because it acts through combination, whereas the person (*puruṣa*) exists for his own sake.
Likewise, the intellect consists of the three *guṇas* because it determines all objects, and because it consists of the three *guṇas*, it is insentient.
The person, however, is the witness of the *guṇas*; therefore, he is not of the same nature [as the intellect].
"Let it be, then, that he is disfigured.
Why is he not utterly disfigured?
Because even though he is pure, he is one who observes conditions.
One perceives the cognition of the Buddha; perceiving that, although not identical in nature to it, one appears as if identical to it.

And so it has been said: "The power of the enjoyer is indeed unchanging and non-transmigrating, yet it seems to have transmigrated into the changing object and follows its modifications. Because it merely mimics that modification of the intellect which has acquired the form of the reflection of consciousness, the cognitive function is described as being indistinguishable from the modification of the intellect. That alone is the self of the visible" (Yogasūtra 2.21).
[YS 2.21] Since the object of sight has assumed the state of being an object for the Puruṣa, whose nature is pure seeing, the very purpose of the object of sight is the self (ātman) of that [Puruṣa].
The meaning is that it becomes its own essential nature (svarūpa).

However, its own nature (svarūpa), having acquired its identity through the form of the other (the intellect), is no longer perceived by the Puruṣa once the purposes of experience and liberation have been accomplished.
Thus, it would follow that there is destruction of this [nature] due to the loss of its own form; yet, it does not perish.
Why?
"Though destroyed for one whose purpose has been fulfilled, it is not destroyed because it is common to others" (YS 2.22).
For one person whose purpose has been fulfilled, the object of perception, though destroyed— meaning it has reached its end— is not destroyed, because it remains common to other persons.

Even though it has met with destruction in the case of a virtuous person, it does not have its purpose fulfilled in the case of non-virtuous persons; thus, according to their view, it indeed attains its own form through the form of another when it has entered the objective domain of the act of seeing.
And for this reason, because the powers of seeing and the seer are eternal, their conjunction is explained as being beginningless.
As it has been said: "Because there is a beginningless conjunction of substrates, there is also a beginningless conjunction of mere attributes."
With the desire to explain the essential nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), this aphorism was set forth:
"Conjunction is the cause for the perception of the essential natures of the power of the self and the power of the owner" (YS 2.23).

The Puruṣa, as the master, is conjoined with the object of vision for the purpose of seeing. From that conjunction, whatever perception of the object occurs is experience (bhoga). However, the perception of the seer’s own true nature is liberation (apavarga).
It has been stated that conjunction terminates with the act of seeing; thus, seeing is said to be the cause of disjunction.
Seeing is the antithesis of non-seeing; thus, non-seeing is stated to be the cause of conjunction.
In this context, seeing is not the direct cause of liberation; rather, the absence of bondage—which results solely from the cessation of non-seeing—is what constitutes liberation.

Since the cause of bondage, which is non-perception (*adarśana*), is destroyed when perception (*darśana*) exists, perception—meaning knowledge—is said to be the cause of liberation (*kaivalya*). Furthermore, what is this so-called "non-perception"? Is it the mandate (*adhikāra*) of the *guṇas*, or rather the non-arising of the primary mind (*pradhānacitta*)—which has the nature of the Seer (*dṛśirūpa*), whose master is the Self, and for whom the object has been shown? It is that absence of perception while its own object of vision (*dṛśya*) is present.
Is it that the qualities (guṇas) possess purposefulness?
Or is it that ignorance (avidyā), having ceased together with one's own mind, is the seed for the arising of that very mind?
Is it that upon the exhaustion of the formative forces of stability (sthitisaṃskāra), the formative forces of motion (gatisaṃskāra) become manifest?
Regarding this which has been stated: if the Pradhāna were to exist through stillness alone, it would not be the Pradhāna because it would not produce transformations;
likewise, if it were to exist through motion alone, it would not be the Pradhāna because its transformations would be eternal.
Its activity, however, acquires the designation "Pradhāna" only when it functions in both ways, and not otherwise.
The same analysis applies even if other causes are postulated.
Some maintain that non-perception is simply the power of perception itself, based on the scriptural statement: "The activity of Pradhāna is for the sake of manifesting its own Self.

[They argue that] prior to activity, the Puruṣa, though capable of cognizing all objects of cognition, does not see; likewise, the object of vision (dṛśya), though capable of performing all functions, is not seen at that time.
Some maintain that non-perception belongs to both [the seer and the seen].
In this regard, although perception is the very nature of the object of sight, it becomes a property of the object of sight only in dependence upon the cognition of the Puruṣa.
Likewise, although non-perception is not the nature of the Puruṣa, it appears as a property of the Puruṣa in dependence upon the cognition of the object of sight.
Some maintain that vision is indeed knowledge, while non-vision is [the absence thereof].
These are the various conceptual positions found in the treatises.
Among them, this multiplicity of views concerns the common objects resulting from the conjunction of the *guṇas* with all *puruṣas*.
But as for that conjunction of the conscious self with its own intellect,
its cause is ignorance (avidyā). [YS 2.24] [YS 2.24]
The meaning is "the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of erroneous cognition.

Furthermore, a *buddhi* permeated by the latent impressions of erroneous cognition does not reach the finality of its task, which is the discernment of the *puruṣa*; it returns again, as it still possesses its functional mandate (*sādhikārā*). However, that [other *buddhi*] reaches the finality of its task, which culminates in the discernment of the *puruṣa*. Having fulfilled its mandate and with non-perception having ceased, it does not return again due to the absence of the cause of bondage.

On this point, someone introduces the illustration of the eunuch (*paṇḍaka*): A foolish wife says, "Noble son, my sister has offspring; why is it that I do not? He replies to her, "I am dead; I shall produce offspring for you.

Likewise, this existing knowledge does not bring about the cessation of the mind; what hope is there that it will do so once it has perished? Regarding this, a teacher-like person says: "Is not liberation simply the cessation of the intellect (*buddhi*), [which occurs] through the absence of the cause of non-perception? Thus, there is the cessation of the intellect."
And that non-perception, which is the cause of bondage, ceases through perception.
In this regard, liberation is simply the cessation of the mind; why then does this delusion of his intellect occur regarding what is not the case?
It has been stated that suffering is to be abandoned and its cause—known as conjunction—is accompanied by its instrumental conditions; therefore, abandonment must now be explained.
"From the absence of that [non-perception], there is the absence of conjunction; this is 'abandonment,' which is the isolation of the seer.

(YS 2.25) The meaning is that from the absence of that non-perception, there is the absolute cessation of the conjunction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*), which is the end of bondage.
This is abandonment (*hāna*). For one who perceives that, it means isolation (*kaivalya*), the non-mixture of the *puruṣa*, and the absence of further conjunction with the *guṇas*.
When the cause of suffering has ceased, the cessation of suffering is abandonment; at that time, it is said that the *puruṣa* is established in its own nature.
Now, what is the means for attaining abandonment?—
the means for abandonment is undisturbed discriminative discernment (vivekakhyāti).
The discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is the cognition of the distinctness between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*.
However, as long as false knowledge has not been ceased, it fluctuates.

When false knowledge becomes like a burnt seed—rendered incapable of fruiting—then for the *sattva* whose dust of afflictions has been shaken off, which abides in supreme clarity and in the highest state known as "mastery," the flow of discriminative cognition becomes stainless.
That discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), when undisturbed, is the means for cessation.
From that follows the attainment of the state of burnt seeds for false knowledge, and thus its non-reproduction; this is the path to liberation, the means for cessation.
Its wisdom (*prajñā*) has seven stages of culmination.
[YS 2.27] "Of that" is a reference back to one for whom discriminative knowledge has arisen.
"Sevenfold" means that when the impurities of the veil of impurity have been removed and no other mental modifications arise, the discerning person's wisdom becomes sevenfold.
That is to say: that which was to be fully understood has been fully understood; there is nothing further for him to fully understand.
The causes of what is to be abandoned have been exhausted; there is nothing further for these to be exhausted.
Abandonment has been realized through the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*).
"The means of liberation, which consists of discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), has been cultivated.
This fourfold liberation belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*).
However, the threefold liberation of the mind (*citta*) is the intellect (*buddhi*) whose functional mandate has been fulfilled.
The *guṇas*, like stones fallen from the slopes of a mountain peak, are unstable; facing dissolution, they set along with their own cause.
And for these dissolved [guṇas], there is no further arising, due to the absence of any purpose.
In this state, the *puruṣa* is solitary (*kevalī*), having transcended the connection with the *guṇas*, stainless, and consisting solely of the light of its own essential nature.
A person who contemplates this sevenfold wisdom of the ultimate stage is called "skilled.
Even upon the withdrawal of the mind, he remains "liberated" and "skilled" because he has transcended all qualities (*guṇa*).
Thus, discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is established as the means of cessation. And since no accomplishment occurs without a means, this [treatise] is now commenced.
From the practice of the limbs of yoga, upon the destruction of impurity, there arises the illumination of knowledge up to discriminative discernment.
(YS 2.28) The eight limbs of yoga are those that will be described hereafter.
From the performance of these [practices], there is the destruction—that is, the elimination—of the fivefold impurity which consists of their opposites.
Upon that destruction, right knowledge becomes manifest.
And to the extent that the means are practiced, to that same extent the impurity undergoes attenuation.
And in whatever measure [the impurity] is diminished, in that same measure the radiance of knowledge increases, following the sequence of that diminution.
This very increase reaches its culmination until the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), meaning up to the thorough knowledge of the essential natures of the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*.
The practice of the limbs of yoga is the cause for the dissociation from impurity.

Just as an axe is the cause for that which is to be cut, so too discriminative discernment has attainment as its cause— just as virtue is the cause of happiness— and not otherwise. And how many such causes are there in the treatise?
He says that there are exactly nine. Namely:
"Origination, subsistence, manifestation, modification, cognition, acquisition, separation, change, and support—these are remembered as the ninefold causes."
In this regard, the mind is the cause of the arising of consciousness; the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatā*) is the cause of the persistence of the mind, just as food is for the body.

The cause of manifestation is, for example, light for form, and likewise the cognition of form [is the cause of the manifestation] of form. The cause of modification is another object for the mind, just as fire is for that which is to be cooked.
The cognition of smoke is the causal condition for the cognition of fire.
The practice of the limbs of yoga is the cause of attainment for discriminative discernment. That same practice is the cause of disjunction from impurity.

The cause of transformation is, for example, a goldsmith in relation to gold; likewise, for a single object that serves as a condition for a woman, ignorance is the cause of delusion, hatred of suffering, passion of pleasure, and knowledge of reality of equanimity.
The cause of support is the body for the sense organs.

And those great elements (mahābhūta) belong to bodies; and all of them—whether belonging to animals, humans, or gods—are mutually related to one another because they serve each other's purposes. Thus, there are nine causes.
These should also be applied, as far as possible, to other categories of things.
The practice of the limbs of yoga, however, serves as a cause in two ways.
In this regard, the limbs of yoga are defined:
"Yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi are the eight limbs" (YS 2.29).
[YS 2.29] We shall explain their practice and their essential nature in due order.
Among these—
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the restraints (yamāḥ).
Among these, non-violence is the absence of malice toward all beings in every way and at all times.

Furthermore, the subsequent restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) are rooted in that [non-violence]; they are taught solely for the purpose of establishing it, with the intent of achieving its perfection.
They are undertaken precisely for the sake of making its form pure.

And so it has been said: "Indeed, as this Brahmin increasingly desires to undertake many vows, so he turns away from the causes of violence committed through negligence, thereby making that very non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) of a pure form."
Truth (*satya*) consists of speech and mind directed toward reality.
That is, speech and mind should correspond exactly to what has been seen and what has been inferred.
Speech is uttered for the purpose of transferring one's own understanding to another; provided that it is not deceptive, erroneous, or barren of comprehension.

This [speech] is intended for the benefit of all beings, not for the injury of beings. And if, even when spoken thus, it were intent upon injuring beings, it would not be truth; it would be merely evil. Through that semblance of merit, that counterfeit of merit, one would fall into miserable darkness.
Therefore, having examined what is beneficial to all beings, one should speak the truth.

Theft (*steya*) is the appropriation of another's property not in accordance with the scriptures; its prohibition, moreover, is non-stealing (*asteya*), which consists of the absence of desire for such things.

Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the restraint of the organ of generation when the senses are guarded. Non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*) is the refusal to accept objects due to perceiving the defects in their acquisition, preservation, loss, attachment, and the injury caused thereby. These are the restraints (*yamāḥ*).
But those [observances],
unrestricted by class, place, time, or circumstance, being universal in scope, constitute the Great Vow (mahāvrata).
In this context, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) delimited by species is, for a fisherman, violence only toward fish and not toward anything else.

That same [non-violence] delimited by place is: "I shall not kill at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). That same [non-violence] delimited by time is: "I shall not kill on the fourteenth day, nor on an auspicious day."

That same [non-injury] is restricted by three factors for one who has desisted from it: it is limited by occasion, such as "I shall not kill for the sake of gods or Brahmins, nor otherwise. And just as for Kṣatriyas, injury is restricted to battle alone and not elsewhere, so too non-injury and the other virtues must be observed in every way when they are not restricted by caste, place, time, or occasion.
Those that are never known to deviate in any way across all stages and all objects are called the "universal great vows" (*sārvabhauma-mahāvratas*).
Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (*niyamas*) [Yogasūtra 2.32].

In this context, purity (*śauca*) consists of external purification produced by earth, water, and so forth, as well as the consumption of pure substances; internal purity is the washing away of the impurities of the mind.
Contentment (*saṃtoṣa*) is the lack of desire for more than the means already at hand.
Austerity (*tapas*) is the endurance of the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*).
These pairs are hunger and thirst, cold and heat, standing and sitting, and silence like a log as well as silence through gesture.
Their observances (*vrata*) are, as appropriate, the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, *sāṃtapana*, and so forth.
Self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the study of the scriptures on liberation or the recitation of the *praṇava*.
Devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) is the dedication of all actions to Him, the Supreme Teacher.
Whether lying on a bed, sitting, or walking on a path, one who is composed and whose web of discursive thoughts has been destroyed—
Perceiving the destruction of the seed of saṃsāra, one should remain ever-yoked and partake in the enjoyment of the immortal.

Regarding that which was stated: "From these, there arises the realization of the inward-turned consciousness and the absence of obstacles," it follows that for these restraints (yama) and observances (niyama):
"When obstructed by discursive thoughts (vitarka), one should cultivate their opposites" (Yoga Sūtra 2.33).

[YS 2.33] When such vitarkas (unwholesome thoughts) as violence arise for this Brahmin— such as, "I shall kill the wrongdoer," "I shall speak falsehood," "I shall take his property," "I shall be unchaste with his wife," or "I shall become the master of his possessions"— and when he is afflicted by the intensely blazing fever of vitarkas tending toward the wrong path, he should cultivate their opposites.
"Being cooked in the terrible embers of saṃsāra, I have taken refuge in the yoga-dharma which grants fearlessness to all beings.
Indeed, I should reflect that by abandoning those very discursive thoughts (vitarka) and then taking them up again, I am equal to the conduct of a dog.
Just as a dog licks what has been vomited, so too am I one who takes back what has been abandoned."
This and other such points should also be applied to other sūtras.

For discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) such as violence and the like—whether performed, caused to be performed, or approved; whether preceded by greed, anger, or delusion; and whether mild, moderate, or intense—have suffering and ignorance as their endless fruits; thus is the cultivation of the counteragent (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*).

In that regard, violence (*hiṃsā*) is first of three kinds: committed, caused to be committed, or approved. Each of these, in turn, is threefold: [committed] out of greed for the sake of meat or skin; out of anger, thinking "this person has done me harm"; or out of delusion, thinking "there will be merit for me. Furthermore, greed, anger, and delusion are each of three degrees: mild, medium, and intense.
Thus, there are twenty-seven varieties of violence.
Furthermore, these are threefold—mild, medium, and intense—namely: mild-mild, medium-mild, and intense-mild;
likewise, mild-medium, medium-medium, and intense-medium.
Likewise, there are the mild-intense, the medium-intense, and the excessive-intense.
Thus, violence consists of eighty-one varieties.
Furthermore, it becomes innumerable through the distinctions of restriction (*niyama*), option (*vikalpa*), and combination (*samuccaya*), because the varieties of living beings are beyond counting.
The same should be applied to falsehood and the other [unwholesome roots] as well.
Indeed, these discursive thoughts have suffering and ignorance as their infinite results; this is the cultivation of the antidote.
That is, the cultivation of the antidote consists in [recognizing] those for which suffering and ignorance are the infinite results.
And so, first of all, the assailant strikes away the victim's vitality;
then he causes him pain by the falling of weapons and the like;
and finally, he deprives him even of life.
Then, due to the exhaustion of his vigor, his animate and inanimate implements lose their potency.

Because he has caused suffering, he experiences pain in the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and so forth. Because he has deprived others of life, he remains at every moment on the brink of death; even though he desires to die, because the ripening of that karma must necessarily be experienced, he somehow barely breathes. And if that act of violence were somehow associated with merit, then upon the attainment of happiness there, he would be short-lived.
In this same way, [the consequences] should be applied to falsehood and the other [unwholesome roots] as far as possible.
Likewise, by contemplating this very undesirable ripening that follows upon discursive thoughts (*vitarka*), one should not direct the mind toward such thoughts.
When, through the cultivation of their antidotes, these discursive thoughts become incapable of arising for him, then the mastery resulting from that indicates the success of the yogin.
For example:
"When non-violence is firmly established, hostility ceases in its presence" (YS 2.35).
This applies to all living beings.
When truth is firmly established, there is the state of being the basis for the fruits of actions.
Thinking, "May he become righteous," he becomes righteous; thinking, "May you attain heaven," he attains heaven; his word becomes unfailing.
Upon the firm foundation of non-stealing, all jewels present themselves [to him].
Jewels from all directions attend upon him.
Through steadfastness in celibacy, there is the attainment of vigor.
By the attainment of which one enhances unimpeded qualities;

and having attained it, one becomes capable of instilling knowledge in those to be trained. Through steadiness in non-possessiveness comes the thorough understanding of the nature of one's births. (Yoga Sūtra 2.39)

[YS 2.39] There arises in him the inquiry into the nature of the self regarding the past, the future, and the middle: "Who was I? How was I? What indeed is this? How indeed is this? And who shall we become? Or how shall we become?
Thus, through the stability of *yama*, these perfections arise in their own form.
We shall explain the observances (*niyama*s):
"From purity comes disgust for one's own body and non-association with others" (YS 2.40).
One who undertakes purification out of disgust for his own limbs becomes an ascetic who perceives the body as faulty and is free from attachment to the body.

Furthermore, being unassociated with others and observing the true nature of the body, even while desiring to abandon his own body and washing it with earth, water, and so forth, he sees no purity in the body; how then could he associate with the bodies of others, which are utterly impure?
Moreover—
"Purity of being, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery of the senses, and fitness for the vision of the Self" (YS 2.41)—
the completion of the sentence is that "these come to be."

From purity comes purification of the *sattva*; from that, cheerfulness; from that, one-pointedness; from that, mastery over the senses; and from that, the fitness of the *buddhi-sattva* for the vision of the Self—this is attained through the steadiness of purity.
From contentment comes the attainment of unsurpassed happiness.
And so it has been said:
"Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is—these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the pleasure that comes from the exhaustion of craving.
Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is...
The perfection of the sense of touch does not equal even a sixteenth part of the bliss of the destruction of craving for the Arhat; it results from the exhaustion of impurity through austerity.

As austerity is being performed, it destroys the impurity of the veil; from the removal of that veiling impurity, there arises the perfection of the body, such as *aṇimā* and so forth. Likewise, there is the perfection of the senses, such as hearing and seeing at a distance.
From the study of one's own sacred texts (*svādhyāya*), there is communion with the chosen deity (YS 2.44).
The gods, seers, and perfected beings appear before one who is devoted to the study of sacred texts (svādhyāya), and they assist him in his task.
Accomplishment in samādhi arises from devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna). [YS 2.45]

[YS 2.45] For one who has surrendered all states of being to the Lord, there is the perfection of *samādhi*, by which he knows everything desired— unerringly— in another place, another body, and another time. Consequently, his wisdom perceives things as they truly are.

The restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), along with their attainments, have been explained. We shall now describe the postures (āsanas) and the others; therein: "A posture is steady and comfortable" (YS 2.46).

Namely: the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), the auspicious posture (*bhadrāsana*), the cross-legged posture (*svastika*), the staff posture (*daṇḍāsana*), the supported posture (*sopāśraya*), the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), the crane’s sitting posture (*krauñcaniṣadana*), the elephant’s sitting posture (*hastiniṣadana*), the camel’s sitting posture (*uṣṭraniṣadana*), the balanced posture (*samasaṃsthāna*), the steady-and-easy posture (*sthirasukha*), and the posture as it pleases (*yathāsukha*); these and others such as these.
[These are attained] through relaxation of effort and meditation on infinity [Yoga Sūtra 2.47].
The phrase "it comes to be" is the ellipsis of the sentence. Posture is accomplished through the cessation of effort, by which the body does not tremble;
or, the mind having attained absorption in the Infinite (ananta), it brings about the perfection of posture.
From that follows "non-affliction by the pairs of opposites" (YS 2.48).
[YS 2.48] By mastery of the posture (āsana), one is not overcome by dualities such as cold and heat.
When that [posture] is established, the cessation of the flow of inhalation and exhalation is breath control (prāṇāyāma). [YS 2.49]

[YS 2.49] When mastery of posture has been attained, inhalation (*śvāsa*) is the drawing in of external air, and exhalation (*praśvāsa*) is the expulsion of abdominal air; the cessation of the movement of both, the absence of both, is breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
It, moreover—

The external and internal fluctuations of the breath, observed in terms of place, time, and number, are long and subtle. [YS 2.50] That which consists of the absence of movement preceded by exhalation is the external [breath].
That in which there is an absence of movement preceded by inhalation is the internal [breath].
The third is the state of suspension (*stambha-vṛtti*), wherein there is an absence of both [inhalation and exhalation] due to a single effort.
Just as water placed on a heated stone undergoes contraction on all sides, so too is there a simultaneous absence of movement in both.
All three of these are delimited by space, meaning that their range is defined as "this much is its spatial extent.
They are delimited by time, which means they are circumscribed by the determination of the number of moments (*kṣaṇa*).

They are delimited by numbers: with this many inhalations and exhalations, there is the first upward movement (*udghāta*); likewise, when [the breath] is restrained, with this many [breaths] there is the second upward movement, and similarly the third.

Thus, it is observed to be mild, middling, or intense according to its enumeration. Indeed, when practiced in this way, it becomes long and subtle; and when it transcends both external and internal objects, it is the fourth [limb]. (Yoga Sūtra 2.51)
[YS 2.51] It is projected by being perceived as an external object through place, time, and number;
likewise, it is projected by being perceived as an internal object.
In both cases, it is long and subtle.
Preceded by that [third type], when there is an absence of movement in both [inhalation and exhalation] through the gradual mastery of the stages, that is the fourth breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
The third, however, is the absence of movement not directed toward objects, which, having been undertaken once, is observed through place, time, and number; it is long and subtle.

The fourth, however, is the absence of movement preceded by the projection of both [inhalation and exhalation], resulting from the sequential mastery of the stages through the determination of the objects of inhalation and exhalation; this is the distinction.
Thereupon, the veil over the light is destroyed.
For this yogin who practices breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), that karma which veils discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñānāvaraṇīya*) is destroyed—
of which they say:
"Having shrouded the luminous *sattva* with the great delusion (*mahāmoha*) consisting of a magical net (*indrajāla*), it impels that very [sattva] toward what ought not to be done."
Thus, his karma—which is an obscuration of the light and the cause of bondage to saṃsāra—becomes weakened through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and is destroyed moment by moment.
And so it has been said:
"There is no austerity superior to breath control; from it comes the purification of impurities and the radiance of knowledge."
Furthermore:
"And there is fitness of the mind for the concentrations" (YS 2.53).
[This is achieved] precisely through the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), according to the statement: "Or, by means of exhalation and retention of the breath.
Now, what is withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*)?
"Withdrawal is as it were the imitation by the senses of the nature of the mind when they are not in contact with their own objects" (Yogasūtra 2.54).

[YS 2.54] "In the absence of contact with their respective objects, they seem to conform to the very nature of the mind. When the mind is restrained, the senses are restrained along with it; they do not require any other means, as is the case when one has already conquered the other senses. Just as bees fly up after the king bee when he flies up, and settle down after him when he settles down, so too the senses are restrained when the mind is restrained—this is *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).
Beyond that, there is supreme mastery over the senses [YS 2.55].
Some maintain that the conquest of the senses consists in being free from addiction to sound and other objects of the senses.
"Attachment (sakti) casts one away from the highest good; it is a vice. Therefore, a practice that is not contradictory [to spiritual goals] is the proper course.
Others hold that the engagement with sound and other sense objects according to one's own will [is permissible].
Some maintain that mastery over the senses (*indriyajaya*) consists in the cognition of sound and other objects being devoid of pleasure and pain due to the absence of passion and hatred.
Jaigīṣavya, however, holds that it is simply non-apprehension resulting from one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*).

Furthermore, this is the supreme form of mastery: when the mind is restrained, the senses are likewise restrained, and they do not require any other effortful means as is the case with other forms of sense-mastery for the yogin.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Sādhanapāda, in the illustrious Pātañjala Yogaśāstra, the exposition of Sāṃkhya, the commentary by the venerable Vyāsa. [The Vibhūtipāda:
The five external means of practice have been described.
Concentration (dhāraṇā) must be explained:
"Concentration is the binding of the mind to a location" [YS 3.1].

Dhāraṇā (concentration) is the binding of the mind to locations such as the navel-center, the heart-lotus, the head, the light, the tip of the nose, or the tip of the tongue, or to external objects, by means of the mere activity of the mind.
Therein, the one-pointed flow of cognition is dhyāna (meditation). [YS 3.2]
[YS 3.2] In that place, the one-pointedness of the cognition whose object is the thing to be meditated upon—a continuous flow untouched by other cognitions—is *dhyāna* (meditative absorption).
That same [absorption], when it manifests as the object alone, as if devoid of its own nature, is *samādhi* (concentration). [YS 3.3]

When meditation itself appears in the form of the object of meditation and becomes, as it were, empty of its own nature consisting of the cognitive process due to the absorption into the very essence of the object, then it is called *samādhi*.
The three together in one place constitute *saṃyama*.
[YS 3.4] This triad of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*) constitutes *saṃyama*. These three means directed toward a single object are called *saṃyama*.
The technical definition for this triad is *saṃyama*.
From mastery over it, the light of wisdom arises.

From the mastery of that restraint, there arises illumination through the wisdom of samādhi; to the extent that the restraint becomes firmly established, to that same extent the wisdom of samādhi becomes confident.
Its application is to the stages [of meditative absorption].
The application of that *saṃyama* is to the stage immediately following the stage already mastered.
For one who has not conquered a lower stage cannot attain *saṃyama* regarding the final stages by skipping over the immediately subsequent stage.
And in the absence of that [attainment], how could there be for him the light of wisdom (*prajñāloka*)?

Furthermore, for one who has conquered a higher stage through the grace of the Lord, it is not appropriate to practice *saṃyama* on lower stages, such as the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and so forth.
Why? Because that object [of the lower stage] is already understood from another source.
Regarding the matter of "this stage is immediately followed by that stage," Yoga itself is the teacher.
For how has it been said:
"Yoga is to be known through yoga; yoga proceeds from yoga. He who is heedful by means of yoga will delight in yoga for a long time.
Thus, "yoga is to be known through yoga; yoga proceeds from yoga."
But he who is heedful through yoga delights in yoga for a long time;
these three are internal compared to the previous ones.

Thus, this triad of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* is the internal limb (*antaraṅga*) of cognitive (*saṃprajñāta*) concentration (*samādhi*), as compared to the five previous means beginning with *yama*.
Even that is an external limb (*bahiraṅga*) of seedless (*nirbīja*) concentration.
Even that triad of means, though internal, becomes external to seedless yoga; why? Because it exists only in the absence of that [seedless state].

Now, since the activity of the *guṇas* is mobile during the moments of the mind’s cessation, what kind of transformation of the mind occurs then?—[The answer is: "The transformation of cessation is the suppression of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of emergence and the manifestation of the latent impression of cessation, occurring in a mind that persists through the moments of cessation" (YS 3.9).

[YS 3.9] The *saṃskāras* of emergence (*vyutthāna*) are properties of the mind; they do not consist of cognitive modifications (*pratyaya*). Therefore, when the modifications cease, they are not destroyed. The *saṃskāras* of cessation (*nirodha*) are also properties of the mind. The suppression of the former and the manifestation of the latter occur such that the *saṃskāras* of emergence diminish and the *saṃskāras* of cessation increase. The mind follows the moment of cessation; this change in the nature of the *saṃskāras* of a single mind at every moment is the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of cessation.
At that time, the mind has residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) alone; this was explained in the context of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*).
Its flow becomes tranquil due to those impressions.
(Yogasūtra 3.10)
The mind's state of peaceful flow depends upon the proficiency gained through the practice of cessation and mental formation (*saṃskāra*).
When the force of those formations weakens, the formation characterized by cessation is overcome by the formation belonging to the nature of emergence (*vyutthāna*).
Thus, the transformation of the mind in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) consists in the waning of the capacity for all objects and the arising of one-pointedness. (Yogasūtra 3.11)
[YS 3.11] The state of being directed toward all objects is a property of the mind;
one-pointedness also is a property of the mind.
The meaning is that the destruction of all-objectedness is its disappearance;

the meaning is that the emergence of one-pointedness is its appearance. The mind is the underlying substratum (dharmin) for these two; thus, this very mind, persisting through these two attributes (dharmas) which constitute its own nature—their passing away and their arising—is concentrated. This is the transformation of concentration (samādhi-pariṇāma) of the mind.
Then again,
when the subsided and the arisen have an identical object of cognition, that is the transformation of the mind into one-pointedness.

For one whose mind is concentrated, the preceding cognition is calm and the succeeding one arises similar to it; the mind of concentration follows both, and thus it remains just as it was due to no lapse from concentration.
This, indeed, is the transformation of the mind, the substratum, into one-pointedness.
By this, the transformations of properties (*dharma*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and states (*avasthā*) in the elements and the sense organs are explained. [YS 3.13]

[YS 3.13] By this aforementioned transformation of the mind, consisting of the forms of dharma, laksana, and avastha, it should be understood that the transformation of dharma, the transformation of laksana, and the transformation of avastha have been described with respect to the elements (bhūta) and the sense organs (indriya).
Among these, the suppression of emergence (vyutthāna) and the manifestation of cessation (nirodha) constitute the transformation of dharma within the substratum (dharmin).

The transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapariṇāma*) is cessation characterized by three marks and endowed with the three time-periods (*adhvan*). Indeed, having first abandoned the future characteristic period while not yet having transcended its essential nature (*dharmatva*), it enters the present characteristic period,
wherein its own form becomes manifest.
This is its second path.
Yet it is not devoid of the two characteristics of the past and the future.

Likewise, emergence possesses three characteristics and is endowed with the three paths; having abandoned the characteristic of the present, it has not transcended the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and has entered into the characteristic of the past.
This is its third path.
And it is not devoid of the two characteristics of the future and the present.

Thus, when emerging again and attaining [the state], having abandoned the characteristic of the future, it has entered the characteristic of the present without overstepping its essential nature (*dharmatā*).
That in which its own nature becomes manifest, wherein its activity occurs—this is its second path.
And it is not devoid of the two characteristics of the past and the future;
thus there is again cessation, and thus there is again emergence.

Likewise, there is the transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*). In that regard, during the moments of cessation, the formative forces of cessation (*nirodha-saṃskāra*) become strong, while the formative forces of emergence (*vyutthāna-saṃskāra*) become weak.
This is the transformation of state of phenomena (*dharma*).

In this context, the substratum (*dharmin*) undergoes transformation through its properties (*dharma*); the properties belonging to the three times undergo transformation through their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); and the characteristics themselves undergo transformation through their states (*avasthā*).
Thus, due to the transformations of the characteristics, states, and conditions of the *guṇas*, the functioning of the *guṇas* does not remain still for even a single moment.
And the functioning of the *guṇas* is mobile;
indeed, it has been stated that the inherent nature of the *guṇas* is the cause of their activity.
By this, it should be understood that there is a threefold transformation in the elements and the sense organs due to the distinction between attribute and substrate;
however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is only one transformation.
For an attribute is merely the essential nature of the substrate; it is simply the modification of the substrate itself that is elaborated through the medium of its attributes.

In this regard, for a dharma existing within a substratum (dharmin), there is a change in its state (bhāvānyathātva) across the time-periods of past, future, and present, but not a change in its substance (dravyānyathātva).
Just as when a golden vessel is broken and fashioned into something else, there is a change in its state but no change in the gold itself.
Another says: the substratum is not distinct from its dharmas, because it does not transcend its prior reality.
"If it were a persisting entity, it would revolve as something entirely immutable, without undergoing any distinction between its prior and subsequent states.
This is not a fault.
Why?
Because absolute [non-existence] is not admitted.
Thus, this triple world departs from its manifestation, because permanence is denied;
yet even when it has departed, it still exists, because destruction is denied.
And from association with this [past time], it possesses subtlety; and from subtlety, there is non-perception.

Regarding the transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapariṇāma*): a dharma existing in the time-periods, when present, is endowed with the characteristic of the past, yet not dissociated from the two characteristics of the future and the present.
Likewise, when future, it is endowed with the characteristic of the future, yet not dissociated from the two characteristics of the present and the past.
Thus, while existing [in the present], being endowed with the characteristic of the present, it is not dissociated from the characteristics of the past and the future.
Just as a man who is attached to one woman is not thereby dispassionate toward the rest, so it is here.

Regarding this transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*), opponents raise the objection that because everything would be conjoined with all characteristics, there would result a confusion of the time periods (*adhva-saṃkara*).
The rebuttal to this is as follows: the "dharma-nature" (dharmatva) of phenomena is not something to be established [by you].
And since dharma-nature exists, a distinction between its characteristics must also be stated; it is not the case that its dharma-nature exists only at the present moment.
For if this were so, the mind would not possess the nature of passion (*rāga*), because passion does not manifest at the time of anger.
Furthermore, it is impossible for the three characteristics to exist simultaneously in a single individual;
rather, their manifestation occurs sequentially through their respective manifestors.
And it has been said: "Excellences of form and excellences of function are mutually exclusive, whereas universals coexist with those excellences."

Therefore, there is no confusion; for instance, when passion (*rāga*) itself manifests in a certain case, it does not mean that at that time it is absent elsewhere, but rather that one is simply endowed with it in a general sense. Thus, its existence is present there at that time, and the same applies to the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). The substratum (*dharmī*) does not belong to the three times (*tryadhvan*), whereas the factors (*dharma*) do belong to the three times. Among these, some are characterized (*lakṣita*) and others are uncharacterized (*alakṣita*). Therein, those that are characterized, while reaching various states, are designated as different due to their change of state, not due to a difference in substance (*dravya*).

Just as a single line represents one hundred in the hundreds-place, ten in the tens-place, and one in the units-place; and just as a single woman is called a mother, a daughter, and a sister according to her state.
Regarding the transformation of states (*avasthā-pariṇāma*), some have raised the objection that it would entail the fault of immutability (*kauṭasthya*).
How so?
Because [the three] time periods are separated by activity (*vyāpāra*).

When a phenomenon (*dharma*) does not perform its own activity, it is future; when it performs it, it is present; and when, having performed it, it has ceased, it is past. Thus, the opponents state the fault that the characteristics and the states of both the phenomenon and the substratum (*dharmī*) would result in immutability (*kauṭasthya*). This is not a fault.
Why?
Because, even though the *guṇas* are eternal, there is a variety of their mutual suppression (*vimarda*).

Just as the configuration (*saṃsthāna*)—which is a beginningless property (*dharmamātra*) of the *guṇas* such as sound and so forth that are themselves subject to destruction and non-destruction—is likewise the *liṅga* (the Great Principle), which is a beginningless property of the *guṇas* such as *sattva* and so forth that are subject to destruction and non-destruction; regarding that [liṅga], there is the designation "modification" (*vikāra*).

In this regard, there is this illustration: clay, as a substratum (dharmin), undergoing a transition from one state (dharma) in the form of a lump to another state in the form of a jar, undergoes transformation in terms of its state (dharmapariṇāma).
The jar, having abandoned its future characteristic (lakṣaṇa) and attained its present characteristic, undergoes transformation in terms of its characteristic (lakṣaṇapariṇāma).
The jar, experiencing newness and antiquity at every moment, undergoes transformation in terms of its condition (avasthāpariṇāma).

A different property (*dharma*) of a substrate (*dharmī*) is a state (*avasthā*), and a different characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of a property is also a state; thus, the single transformation of substance (*dravyapariṇāma*) is presented through these distinctions.
This should be applied similarly to other categories as well.

These transformations of properties, characteristics, and states do not transcend the essential nature of the substrate; therefore, there is only one transformation that encompasses all these particularities.
Now, what is this transformation (*pariṇāma*)?
Transformation is the arising of another property (*dharmāntara*) upon the cessation of a previous property of a persisting substance.
In that regard—
The substrate (dharmī) conforms to attributes (dharma) that are quiescent, emergent, or unmanifest.
An attribute is simply the power of the substrate as delimited by its capacity.
And that [substratum], inferred from the differences in the production of its fruits, is observed to be both one and distinct from others.

In that state, the substrate (*dharmin*), while currently undergoing its own activity, is distinguished from other properties (*dharmas*)—namely, those that are quiescent and those that are inexpressible.

But when it is endowed with [properties] in a general sense, then, because it consists of nothing but the essential nature of the substrate itself, what would it be, and by what would it be distinguished?

In this regard, the properties (*dharma*) of a substrate (*dharmī*) are indeed those that are subsided (*śānta*), arisen (*udita*), and indeterminate (*avyapadeśya*). Among these, the subsided are those which, having performed their functions, have ceased; the arisen are those still performing their functions. These [arisen ones] are immediately preceded by the future characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and immediately followed by the present; the past ones are immediately followed by the present. Why are they not immediately preceded by the past? Because there is no priority or posteriority [in the case of the past]. Just as there is priority and posteriority between the future and the present, it is not so for the past.
Therefore, the past has no immediate predecessor; rather, it is the future itself that is the immediate predecessor of the present.
Now, as for those who maintain that the indefinable is everything and that everything has the nature of all things:

it has been stated that the transformative variety of tastes and so forth belonging to water and earth is seen in stationary beings; likewise, the qualities of stationary beings are found in moving beings, and those of moving beings in stationary ones. Thus, without the cessation of their respective classes, everything has the nature of all things.
Indeed, due to the constraints of place, time, form, and cause, the manifestation of the selves does not occur simultaneously.
That which persists through these attributes—whether manifested or unmanifested—and whose nature consists of both the universal and the particular, is the persisting substrate (dharmī).
For one who holds that this is merely a collection of attributes without any persisting substrate, there can be no experience of pleasure or pain.
Why? Because how could one [consciousness] be authorized as the experiencer of an action performed by another consciousness?

Furthermore, there is an absence of memory for that [action], since one person does not remember what was seen by another. And because of the recognition of objects, a persisting substratum (*dharmī*) is established, which is recognized as having undergone a change in its properties (*dharma*); therefore, this is not a mere property (*dharma*) devoid of a persisting substrate.
"Difference in sequence is the cause of difference in transformation" (YS 3.15).
When it might follow that a single substrate has only one transformation, the fact that there is a difference in sequence serves as the reason for the difference in transformation.
For example, the sequence is: powder, a lump of clay, a clay pot, a shard of clay, and a particle of clay.
Whatever phenomenon (dharma) immediately precedes another phenomenon is its sequence.
When the lump ceases and the pot arises, this is the sequence of the transformation of phenomena.
The sequence of the transformation of characteristics is as follows: for a jar, the transition from its future state to its present state is a sequence;
likewise, for the lump of clay, the transition from its present state to its past state is a sequence.
There is no sequence for that which is already past.
Why?
Because immediate succession exists only when there is a relation of priority and posteriority, but that does not exist for the past; therefore, the sequence applies only to two characteristics.
Likewise, the sequence of the transformation of states is also observed: in a new jar, old age is seen at its end.
And that [substance], being manifested through a sequence following a succession of moments, attains a state of supreme manifestation.
This third transformation is distinguished by both its properties (*dharma*) and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
These sequences acquire their own specific forms when there is a distinction between the property and the substratum (*dharmi*).

A property (*dharma*) also becomes a property-bearer (*dharmī*) in relation to the nature of another property. However, when—in ultimate reality—there is a figurative application of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*) such that the property itself is designated by means of that [property-bearer], then this sequence appears precisely as a unity.
Regarding the mind, properties are observed to be of two kinds: those that are perceived and those that are unperceived.

Among these, those consisting of conditions (*pratyaya*) are perceived, while those consisting of mere entities (*vastumātra*) are unperceived. And these latter are exactly seven, their existence as mere entities being established through inference:
"Cessation, duty, mental formations, transformation, and then vitality; activity and power—these are the attributes of the mind that are beyond perception."
Cessation, the properties of conditioned phenomena, transformation, vitality, activity, and power— these are the properties of the mind, devoid of [objective] perception.
Therefore, for the yogin who has mastered all the means of practice, the object of *saṃyama* for the sake of attaining knowledge of the desired object is introduced:
"From *saṃyama* upon the three transformations, there is knowledge of the past and the future" (YS 3.16).

Through *saṃyama* upon the transformations of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the states (*avasthā*), and the essential nature (*pariṇāma*) [of things], knowledge of the past and future arises for yogins.
The triad of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* performed upon a single object is called *saṃyama*.
By means of this, the threefold transformation, being directly realized, brings about knowledge of the past and future regarding those [objects].
Due to the mutual superimposition of word, object, and cognition, there is a confusion among them; by practicing *saṃyama* on their distinction, one gains knowledge of the cries of all beings.
In this regard, speech is meaningful only with respect to the phonemes.

Furthermore, the auditory organ has as its object merely the transformation of sound (*dhvani*). A word (*pada*), however, is to be grasped by a cognition that synthesizes (*anusamhāra*) those sounds (*nāda*). Since phonemes (*varṇa*) cannot occur simultaneously and are therefore mutually independent, they do not touch upon or bring about a word; thus, appearing and disappearing individually, each is said to lack the nature of a word.

Furthermore, each individual phoneme (*varṇa*), being the essence of a word (*padātman*), is infused with the capacity for all denotations; having attained a state of manifoldness (*vaiśvarūpya*) through its relation to other cooperating phonemes, the preceding one is established in a specific [meaning] by the following one, and the following one by the preceding one. Thus, many phonemes, following a sequence and delimited by the convention of meaning—namely, these [three]: the *ga*, the *au*, and the visarga (*visarjanīya*), each enveloped in the capacity for all denotations—illuminate the object characterized by a dewlap and so forth.

Thus, that single mental manifestation which arises from these [phonemes]—which are delimited by the convention of meaning and whose sequence of sounds has been withdrawn—is designated as the "word" (*padam*) that expresses the signified object. That single word is the object of a single cognition, projected by a single effort, partless, without sequence, and devoid of phonemes; it is a mental entity brought forth by the operation of the cognition of the final phoneme. With the desire to convey it to another, it is perceived by listeners—as if already established—through a worldly cognition permeated by the beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of linguistic usage, via the very phonemes being uttered and heard, through a process of conventional consensus.
From that conventional understanding (*saṃketabuddhi*), there arises a distinction: the synthesis (*anusaṃhāra*) of this many such [elements] is the designator of a single object.

However, the convention (*saṃketa*) between word and object consists in mutual superimposition (*itaretarādhyāsa*) and has the nature of memory; namely, "this word is this object" and "this object is this word.
Thus, the convention takes the form of mutual superimposition.
Thus, these—word, object, and cognition—are intermingled through mutual superimposition: "cow" as the word, "cow" as the object, and "cow" as the cognition.
He who knows their distinction is all-knowing.
Furthermore, in every word there is the power of a sentence; when "tree" is uttered, "exists" is understood.
A category does not deviate from its existence;
likewise, there is no action without a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

Thus, when "he cooks" (*pacati*) is said, there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of all the factors of action (*kāraka*); the mention (*anuvāda*) of the agent, instrument, and object—namely Caitra, the fire, and the rice—is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

Furthermore, the arrangement of words is observed within the meaning of a sentence, as in: "The *śrotriya* studies the Veda" (*chandaso 'dhīte*) or "He lives" (*jīvati*), which means he sustains his vital breaths.

In that sentence, the meanings of the individual words are manifested; therefore, having analyzed the word, it must be grammatically explained—whether it denotes an action (*kriyā*) or a participant in the action (*kāraka*).

Otherwise, in cases such as *bhavati*, *aśvaḥ*, or *ajāpayaḥ*, since these resemble both nouns and verbs, how could they be explained as either an action or a participant in the action when their specific nature is not yet determined?
This is the distinction between those [three]: word, object, and cognition.

For example, in the expression "the palace whitens," the word has the sense of an action (*kriyārtha*); in "the white palace," the word has the sense of a factor of action (*kārakārtha*). The object consists of both the action and the factor of action, and the cognition is likewise. Why is this so? Because through the connection "this is that," the cognition takes on a single form; such is the conventional designation (*saṃketa*).
That which is the white object is the objective support (*ālambana*) for both the word and the cognition.
For that [object], as it undergoes modification through its own states, is not accompanied by the word, nor is it accompanied by the cognition.
Thus, the word is one way, the object is another way, and the cognition is yet another way; they are not mutually concomitant—this is the distinction.
Thus, through *saṃyama* on their differentiation, the knowledge of the cries of all beings is attained by the yogi.
From the direct perception of subliminal impressions (*saṃskāra*), knowledge of previous births arises.
(Yoga Sūtra 3.18)

Indeed, these formations (*saṃskāra*) are of two kinds: those whose nature is latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and which serve as the cause of memory and afflictions; and those whose nature is merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) and which serve as the cause of maturation (*vipāka*).

Having been produced by the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of a previous existence, they are mental factors (*cittadharma*) that are imperceptible, like transformation, movement, cessation, potency, and the property of life-force.
Mastery (*saṃyama*) over them is capable of bringing about the direct perception (*sākṣātkriyā*) of those formations.
And there can be no direct realization of those [past lives] without the experience of their place, time, and causes.
Thus, from the direct realization of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), knowledge of previous births arises for the yogin.
Likewise, in other cases as well, through the direct realization of latent impressions, there occurs the perception of other births.

In this regard, the following narrative is heard: As the venerable Jaigīṣavya was observing the sequence of births and transformations throughout ten great cosmic cycles (*mahāsarga*) due to his direct realization of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), knowledge born of discriminative discernment (*vivekaja-jñāna*) arose within him.

Then the venerable Āvaṭya, assuming a subtle body, said to him: "Since you possess a sattva of the intellect that has not been overwhelmed by its own nature due to your auspiciousness throughout ten great cosmic cycles, and since you have clearly perceived the suffering inherent in birth from the wombs of hell-beings and animals, what did you find to be greater among pleasure and pain as you were born again and again among gods and humans?"
Jaigīṣavya said to the Blessed Āvaṭya:

"Throughout ten great cycles of creation, because of my spiritual fitness and because my wisdom and essential nature were never overcome, I have perceived the suffering of existence in the realms of hell and animals; and though I was born again and again among gods and humans, whatever I experienced, I recognize it all as nothing but suffering.
The Blessed Āvaṭya said:
"This supreme mastery over the primary elements and this unsurpassed happiness of contentment belonging to the venerable Jaigīṣavya—why has even this been cast into the category of suffering?
The Lord Jaigīṣavya replied: "This unsurpassed happiness of contentment was described as such only in comparison to the pleasure derived from sense objects.
In comparison to the bliss of liberation (*kaivalya*), it is indeed suffering."
This dharma belongs to the *sattva* of the intellect; it consists of the three *guṇas*, and its corresponding cognition is placed on the side of what is to be abandoned.
It is of the nature of suffering, being a thread of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
However, because of the departure from the torment of the suffering of craving, this [state] is said to be happiness—serene, unassailed, and favorable to all.
[The supernormal power of] knowing another's mind [arises] from the mental modification.
(YS 3.19) By means of *saṃyama* upon the mental modification, through the direct perception of that modification, there arises knowledge of another's mind.
And that [cognition] does not have an object, because that [object] has not become its domain;
one knows the cognition as "attached," but one does not know it as "attached to this particular object."
That which is the object of another's cognition is not made an object by the yogi’s mind; rather, it is merely the other person's cognition that becomes the object for the yogi’s mind.
Through *saṃyama* on the form of the body, when the power of its being perceived is suppressed, there occurs invisibility (*antardhāna*) due to the lack of contact with the light of the eye.
(Yoga Sūtra 3.21)

By restraining the body from form, one obstructs that power of form which is to be grasped. When the power of the object to be grasped is obstructed, and there is no contact with the light of the eye, invisibility arises for the yogin. By this, it should be understood that the invisibility of sound and the other sense objects is likewise described.
Karma is both *sopakrama* (with onset) and *nirupakrama* (without onset); through *saṃyama* upon it, or from the signs of death (*ariṣṭas*), there is knowledge of the end of life.
Karma that ripens as lifespan is of two kinds: *sopakrama* and *nirupakrama*.

In this regard, just as a wet cloth spread out would dry in a shorter time, so it is with that which is accompanied by effort (*sopakrama*). And just as that same cloth, when folded up, would take a long time to dry, so it is with that which is without effort (*nirupakrama*).
Or again, just as a fire set upon dry underbrush, aided by wind from all sides, would burn it in the shortest time, so it is with that which is accompanied by effort.
Or, just as that same fire, when placed gradually upon the parts of a heap of grass, would burn it slowly, so too is the case with the effortless [karma].

That life-determining karma (*āyuṣkara-karma*) pertaining to a single birth is of two kinds: with effort (*sopakrama*) and without effort (*nirupakrama*). Through mastery over that, there arises knowledge of the end, that is, of death.
Regarding the phrase "or from portents," there are three kinds of portents: internal (*ādhyātmika*), external (*ādhibhautika*), and celestial (*ādhidaivika*).
Among these, the internal is when one does not hear the sound within one's own body even with the ears covered, or does not see light even when the eyes are pressed.
Likewise, the external is when one sees the messengers of Yama, or suddenly sees deceased ancestors.
Likewise, one may suddenly see the celestial realm or perfected beings (siddhas), or perceive everything in its opposite; or by this [concentration], one knows that the end of life is at hand.
[The powers regarding] friendliness and so forth [are attained through concentration on them]. (Yoga Sūtra 3.23)

[YS 3.23] There are three meditative cultivations: friendliness, compassion, and gladness. Among these, by cultivating friendliness toward those beings who are happy, one attains the power of friendliness;
by cultivating compassion toward those who are suffering, one attains the power of compassion.
Having cultivated sympathetic joy toward those of virtuous character, one attains the power of sympathetic joy.
The concentration that arises from such cultivation is restraint; from that, powers arise whose vigor is not in vain.
Toward those of evil character, however, there is equanimity, but no cultivation [of joy].

And consequently, since there is no meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in that [state], there is no power (*bala*) derived from equanimity (*upekṣā*), because of the absence of restraint (*saṃyama*) therein.
Regarding the powers, these include the power of an elephant and so forth.
(Yoga Sūtra 3.24) (Yoga Sūtra 3.24)
Through restraint with respect to the strength of an elephant, one becomes possessed of the strength of an elephant;
through restraint with respect to the strength of Vainateya, one becomes possessed of the strength of Vainateya;
through restraint with respect to the strength of the wind, one becomes possessed of the strength of the wind—and so forth.
"Through the application of the light of the cognitive process, there is knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the remote" (YS 3.25).
The cognitive process has been described as luminous; by applying that light of the mind to an object—whether subtle, concealed, or remote—the yogi attains knowledge of that object.
Knowledge of the worlds arises from *saṃyama* on the sun;
its expansion consists of the seven worlds.
Therein, from Avīci up to the summit of Mount Meru is the world of the earth (*bhūrloka*).
Beginning from the summit of Mount Meru up to the Pole Star (*dhruva*) is the intermediate space world (*antarikṣaloka*), variegated with planets, lunar mansions, and stars.
Beyond that is the heavenly world (*svarloka*), the third world, which consists of five types belonging to Mahendra.
The fourth is Maharloka, belonging to Prajāpati.
The realm of Brahmā is threefold, namely: Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka.
"The world of Brahmā consists of three levels; beyond that is the great realm of Prajāpati; and Māhendra is called Svar (heaven). The stars are in the sky, and living beings are on the earth."
The world consisting of three realms is called Brāhma; beyond that is the Mahat, which is Prajāpatya;
and Māhendra is said to be Svar. In heaven there are the stars, and on earth there are living beings.
This is the summary verse.

Therein, situated one above the other, are the grounds of the six great hells—Mahākāla, Ambarīṣa, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Kālasūtra, and Andhatāmisra—which rest respectively upon solid water, fire, wind, space, and darkness.
It is there that living beings, having endured the suffering acquired through their own karma and having drawn out a miserable, long lifespan, are born.
Beyond that are the seven netherworlds known as Mahātala, Rasātala, Talātala, Sutala, Vitala, Talātala, and Pātāla.

This is the eighth level, the earth consisting of seven continents, in the center of which stands Sumeru, the golden king of mountains. Its peaks are composed of silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, gold, and precious gems.

There, due to the coloring by the light of lapis lazuli, the southern portion of the sky is dark like the petal of a blue lotus; the eastern is white; the western is transparent; and the northern has the hue of the *kuraṇṭaka* flower.
On its southern side stands the Jambu tree, from which this is called Jambūdvīpa.
Due to the movement of the sun across it, night and day proceed as if joined together.
To its north are three mountains with blue and white peaks, each two thousand [yojanas] in length.
Between them are three regions, each nine thousand yojanas in extent: Ramaṇaka, Hiraṇmaya, and Uttarakuru.
To the south are the Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat mountains, each two thousand [yojanas] in length.
In the intervals between these are three regions, each nine thousand *yojanas* in extent: Harivarṣa, Kimpuruṣa, and Bhārata.
To the east of Sumeru are Bhadrāśva, bounded by the Mālyavat mountain; to the west are Ketumāla, bounded by the Gandhamādana mountain;
and in the middle is the region of Ilāvṛta.
This [system] extends for a hundred thousand *yojanas* around Sumeru in every direction, with half that distance [from the center].
This Jambūdvīpa, which is indeed one hundred thousand [yojanas] in extent, is encircled by the Salt Ocean, which is twice its size and shaped like a ring.

Beyond that, the continents of Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmala, Gomeda (Plakṣa), Puṣkara, and so forth, each double the size of the preceding, as well as the oceans—which are like heaps of mustard seeds, adorned with various mountain-ornaments, and filled with sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, whey, milk, and sweet water—each likewise double in size.
Surrounded by seven oceans, ring-shaped, and encircled by the Lokāloka mountain range, these [worlds] are numbered at fifty koṭis of yojanas.
All this is arranged within the center of the well-established cosmic egg (aṇḍa).
And this egg is a minute part of Pradhāna, just as a firefly is in the sky.

There, in Pātāla, in the ocean, and upon these mountains, dwell the hosts of gods—Asuras, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Kiṃpuruṣas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Apasmārakas, Apsarases, Brahma-rākṣasas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and Vināyakas.
