In all the continents dwell meritorious gods and humans.
Sumeru is the pleasure garden of the Thirty-three; therein are the gardens known as Miśravana, Nandana, Caitraratha, and Sumānasa.
The Sudharmā is the assembly hall of the gods; Sudarśana is the city; Vaijayanta is the palace.
As for the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, they are fastened to Dhruva and revolve in the sky above Sumeru, their movements characterized by the regulation of the dispersal of the winds.
The six classes of deities residing in the world of Mahendra are: the Tridaśas, Agniṣvāttas, Yāmyas, Tuṣitas, Aparinirmitavaśavartins, and Parinirmitavaśavartins.

All of them have their desires fulfilled by mere thought, are endowed with sovereign powers such as *aṇimā*, live for the duration of a *kalpa*, are gods (*vṛndāraka*), enjoy sensual pleasures, possess bodies born of spontaneous generation (*aupapādikadeha*), and are attended upon by Apsarases who are most excellent and compliant.
In the great world of Prajāpati, there is a fivefold class of deities: the Kumudas, Ṛbhavas, Pratardanas, Añjanābhas, and Pracitābhas.
These masters of the great elements subsist on meditation and have a lifespan of a thousand kalpas.
In the first Janaloka of Brahmā, there are four classes of divine beings: the Brahmapurohitas, the Brahmakāyikas, the Mahābrahmakāyikas, and the Amaras.
They master the elements and the sense faculties, and their lifespans increase twofold for each successive class.

In the second *tapas* world, there are three classes of deities: the Ābhāsvaras, the Mahābhāsvaras, and the Satyamahābhāsvaras. They have mastery over the elements (*bhūta*), the senses (*indriya*), and primordial nature (*prakṛti*); their lifespans increase twofold at each successive level; they all subsist on meditation (*dhyāna-āhāra*); their vital energy flows upward (*ūrdhvaretas*); their knowledge is unimpeded above and their range of knowledge is unobstructed regarding the lower planes. In the third [world], Brahmā’s Satyaloka, there are four classes of deities who do not construct abodes, who are self-supported, situated one above the other, who have mastery over primordial nature (*pradhāna*), and whose lifespan lasts until the end of the creation.

Among them, the Acyutas possess the bliss of dhyāna accompanied by vitarka; the Śuddhanivāsas possess the bliss of dhyāna accompanied by vicāra; the Satyābhās possess the bliss of dhyāna consisting of mere bliss (ānanda); and the Saṃjñāsaṃjñins possess the bliss of dhyāna consisting of mere I-consciousness (asmitā).
They too abide within the midst of the three worlds.
These seven worlds are all indeed the Brahma-worlds.
However, those who have dissolved into the *prakṛti* of Videha abide in the state of liberation; thus, they are not placed in the midst of the worlds.

This must be directly realized by the yogi by performing *saṃyama* on the gate of the sun (*sūryadvāra*). Then, he should likewise practice elsewhere until all this has been seen. [Yoga Sūtra 3.27: "By [saṃyama] on the moon, there is knowledge of the arrangement of the stars."
[YS 3.27] By performing *saṃyama* on the moon, one may know the arrangement of the stars. [YS 3.28] On the pole star (*dhruva*), there is knowledge of their motion.

[YS 3.28] Then, having practiced *saṃyama* on the pole star (*dhruva*), one should know the motion of the stars; having practiced *saṃyama* on the celestial chariots (*ūrdhvavimāna*), one should know them.
[YS 3.29] Through *saṃyama* on the navel-center (*nābhicakra*), there is knowledge of the body's internal structure (*kāyavyūha*).
[YS 3.29] By performing *saṃyama* on the navel-center (*nābhicakra*), one should know the arrangement of the body (*kāyavyūha*). There are three humors (*doṣa*): wind, bile, and phlegm.

There are seven constituent elements (*dhātu*): skin, blood, flesh, sinews, bone, marrow, and semen. Among these, each preceding element is external to the one following it; such is their arrangement.
Cessation of hunger and thirst occurs at the pit of the throat (YS 3.30).
Below the tongue is a fiber; below the fiber is the throat; and below that is the pit. Through *saṃyama* upon that, hunger and thirst do not afflict one.
"Stability through the tortoise-channel" (YS 3.31).
Below the well in the chest is a channel shaped like a tortoise; one who practices *saṃyama* upon it attains a stable state, just as a snake or a lizard does.
"Vision of the Siddhas occurs when there is concentration on the light in the head" (YS 3.32).
Within the cranial vault, there is a luminous aperture; by performing *saṃyama* upon that light, one gains vision of the Siddhas who move in the space between heaven and earth.
Or, everything [is known] through intuition (prātibha).
Intuition is called "the deliverer" (tāraka); it is the precursor to the knowledge born of discrimination.
Just as there is radiance at the rising of the sun, by that [radiance], the yogi knows everything upon the arising of intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-jñāna*).
[In this state,] there is consciousness of the mind within the heart. (YS 3.34)
[YS 3.34] That which is this small lotus-palace within this city of Brahman—therein is consciousness; through *saṃyama* upon that, there is knowledge of the mind.

Experience (*bhoga*) is the non-distinction of the cognitions of the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, which are absolutely unmixed; from *saṃyama* upon one's own nature, as distinct from that which exists for another, comes knowledge of the *puruṣa*. [YS 3.35]

[YS 3.35] The *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is by nature luminous, having brought under control *rajas* and *tamas* through its connection with an equal *sattva*, undergoes transformation by means of the discernment that distinguishes between *sattva* and the Puruṣa.
And the Puruṣa is absolutely distinct from that transforming *sattva*; it is pure, other, and consists solely of the nature of consciousness (*citimātra*).

Between these two [sattva and puruṣa], which are absolutely unmixed, the non-distinction of the cognition is experience (*bhoga*) for the puruṣa, because its object has been presented; that cognition of experience belongs to *sattva* and is an object of sight (*dṛśya*), because it exists for the sake of another.
But as for that distinct, other, puruṣic cognition, whose nature is pure consciousness (*citimātra*), through *saṃyama* upon that, knowledge having the puruṣa as its object arises.

And the puruṣa is not seen by means of the puruṣic cognition which consists of the *buddhi-sattva*; rather, the puruṣa itself perceives that cognition as resting upon its own self. Thus it has been said: "By what, my dear, could one know the knower?"
From that, intuitive insight, hearing, touch, sight, taste, and the sense of smell arise (YS 3.36).
Through intuitive insight (*prātibha*), there arises knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, the remote, the past, and the future.
From hearing [the sound], there is the hearing of divine sounds;
from feeling, the attainment of divine touch;
from seeing, the cognition of divine forms; from tasting, the cognition of divine tastes; and from smelling, the perception of divine fragrances—these arise constantly.
These are obstacles in concentration (*samādhi*) and accomplishments (*siddhi*) in emergence (*vyutthāna*).

[YS 3.37] Those [powers], such as intuitive insight (*prātibha*), when arising for one whose mind is concentrated, are obstacles because they are contrary to that vision; when arising for one whose mind has emerged from concentration, they are accomplishments.
"Entry into another's body occurs through the loosening of the cause of bondage and through the awareness of the movement of the mind" (YS 3.38).

The meaning is this: for the mind that has become liquefied and is without a fixed support, "bondage" is its stabilization within a body due to the force of the latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*). The "loosening" of that karma, which is the cause of bondage, occurs through the power of *samādhi*.

The perception of the movement of the mind arises precisely from meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Through the destruction of the bondage of karma and through the perception of the movement of his own mind, the yogi draws the mind out from his own body and places it within other bodies.
Once the mind has been placed there, the sense organs follow it;
just as bees fly up after the king bee when he flies up, and settle down after him when he settles down, so too do the sense organs conform to the mind during the entry into another body.
From mastery over *udāna*, there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and the like, as well as the power of upward departure.

Life is the functioning of all the senses, characterized by the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth; its fivefold activity consists of *prāṇa*, which moves through the mouth and nose and functions up to the heart.
Because it leads [the breath] equally, *samāna* functions up to the navel;

because it carries away, *apāna* functions down to the soles of the feet; because it leads upward, *udāna* functions up to the head; and *vyāna* is all-pervasive. Of these, *prāṇa* is the primary one. Through mastery over *udāna*, there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and the like, and at the time of death, the departure [of the soul] occurs; he attains mastery over that.
From the mastery of the *samāna* [breath], there is blazing.
[YS 3.40] Having mastered the *samāna*, one performs the kindling of the vital energy (*tejas*) and causes it to blaze forth.
Through *saṃyama* on the connection between the ear and space, divine hearing arises.

Space is the support of all ears and of all sounds; as it has been said: "For all those who hear, though their locations are equal, there is a single locus of hearing for all"—and this is a mark (*liṅga*) of space.
And it has been stated that [space] is unobstructed.
Likewise, because that which is formless is seen to be unobstructed, the all-pervasiveness of space is also well-known.
The auditory faculty is inferred from the perception of sound.

Of the deaf and the non-deaf, one perceives sound while the other does not; therefore, the auditory organ alone has sound as its object. For the yogi who has practiced *saṃyama* upon the connection between the ear and space, the divine ear functions.
Through *saṃyama* on the connection between the body and space, and by attaining mastery over lightness like that of cotton, the power of traveling through space arises.
(Yoga Sūtra 3.42)

Where there is a body, there is space, because space provides room for the body; thus, the connection or acquisition of the body with that [space] is the object of constraint. Having mastered that connection, and having attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in light things such as cotton down, down to the level of atoms, one whose connection has been mastered becomes light.

And due to this lightness, one walks upon water with the feet; then, having walked upon a mere spider’s thread, one walks upon the rays of light; thereafter, one's movement through space occurs at will. External non-imagined functioning is the "Great Bodiless" (*mahāvideha*); from that, there is the destruction of the veil of illumination (*prakāśāvaraṇa*). (Yogasūtra 3.43)
[YS 3.43] The attainment of the functioning of the mind outside the body is the concentration known as "bodiless" (*videha*).
If this occurs merely through the external functioning of the mind while it remains established within the body, it is called "imagined" (*kalpita*).

However, that external functioning of the mind which is independent of the body and occurs solely externally is indeed the unconstructed (*akalpita*). By means of that constructed (*kalpita*) [meditation], one accomplishes that unconstructed state known as the Great Bodilessness (*mahāvideha*), by which yogis enter the bodies of others. Furthermore, from that concentration (*dhāraṇā*), there occurs the destruction of the threefold veil—consisting of afflictions, karma, and their fruition—which obscures the luminous nature of the *buddhi-sattva* and is rooted in *rajas* and *tamas*. Through *saṃyama* upon the gross, essential nature, subtle, inherence, and purposefulness [of the elements], mastery over the elements is attained (YS 3.44).

[YS 3.44] Among these, the specific qualities such as sound and so forth belonging to earth and the other elements, together with their attributes such as shape and so on, are designated by the term "gross" (*sthūla*); this is the first form of the elements.

The second form is their own commonality (*svasāmānya*): solidity is earth, moisture is water, heat is fire, motility is air, and all-pervadingness is space; this is expressed by the term "essential nature" (*svarūpa*).

Sound and the other [qualities] are the particulars (*viśeṣa*) of this universal (*sāmānya*); thus it has been said: "For these things which are endowed with a single genus, there is the exclusion of mere properties.

Here, a substance (*dravya*) is a collection of universals and particulars. For a collection is found in two ways: either as one in which the distinct parts have disappeared, such as a body, a tree, a herd, or a forest; or as one in which the parts remain distinct.

A collection (*samūha*) that follows parts whose distinctions are conveyed by a word— such as "both gods and humans"— is denoted by those two very [parts] as a collection, wherein the gods constitute one part and the humans a second part.

And that [collection] is intended to be expressed in terms of both difference and non-difference, as in "an orchard of mangoes" (*āmrāṇāṃ vanaṃ*) or "an assembly of Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇānāṃ saṃghaḥ*), [which are expressed as] "mango-orchard" (*āmravana*) and "Brahmin-assembly" (*brāhmaṇasaṃgha*).

Furthermore, that [whole] is of two kinds: that whose parts are separately established (*yutasiddhāvayava*) and that whose parts are inseparably established (*ayutasiddhāvayava*). A collection whose parts are separately established is, for example, a "forest" or an "assembly. A collection whose parts are inseparably established is, for example, a "body," a "tree," or an "atom. Patañjali has stated that a substance (*dravya*) is a collection accompanied by the distinction of its inseparably established parts; this is what is called its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Now, what is their subtle form? It is the *tanmātra*, the cause of the elements; a single part of that is the atom (*paramāṇu*). A collection which consists of both the general and the particular, and which follows from the distinction of inseparable parts—this applies to all *tanmātras*. This is the third [form]. Now, the fourth form of the elements is the *guṇas*, whose natures are manifestation (*khyāti*), activity (*kriyā*), and stability (*sthiti*); they are said by the term "concomitance" (*anvaya*) because they follow the nature of their effects. Now, their fifth form is "possessing purpose" (*arthavattva*); the fact that the *guṇas* have the purpose of experience and liberation (*bhoga-apavarga*) is inherent in them alone, and since the *guṇas* exist in the *tanmātras*, the elements, and the elemental products, everything possesses purpose.
Now, from *saṃyama* upon those five elements in their fivefold forms, there arises the vision of the true nature (*svarūpa*) of each form and mastery over it.

Having conquered the five essential natures of the elements therein, one becomes a conqueror of the elements. Through that conquest, the primal natures (*prakṛti*) of the elements become compliant with his will, like cows following their calves.
From that follows the manifestation of the powers such as *aṇiman*, the perfection of the body, and non-obstruction by the properties of those elements. [YS 3.45]
[YS 3.45] Therein, *aṇimā* is that one becomes minute; *laghimā* is that one becomes light; *mahimā* is that one becomes great.
*Prāpti* is that with the very tip of one's finger one touches the moon.
Irresistible will (*prākāmya*) is the non-obstruction of one's desire; [the yogi] emerges from the earth and sinks into it as if in water.

Mastery (*vaśitva*) is being the controller over the elements and elemental products, while others are not the controllers. Sovereignty (*īśitṛtva*) is to exercise power over their origin, dissolution, and arrangement.

The state of having desires fulfilled at will (*yatra-kāmāvasāyitva*) is the reality of one's resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatā*), such that the fundamental natures of the elements abide exactly according to one's resolve.

And even though he is capable, he does not cause a reversal of objects; why? Because another [being] who is previously established and possesses the power of determining objects at will has already formed such a resolve regarding those things.
These are the eight perfections of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

The perfection of the body, which will be described later, and the non-obstruction by its qualities, means that the earth does not obstruct the yogin’s bodily movements and so forth by virtue of its solid form; he can even pass through a stone.

Moist waters do not wet him; the hot fire does not burn him; the blowing wind does not carry him away. Even in space, which is by nature unobstructed, his body becomes obstructed; he becomes invisible even to the perfected ones (*siddhas*).
Beauty of form, loveliness, strength, and adamantine compactness constitute the perfection of the body (*kāyasampat*).
[The yogin becomes] beautiful to behold, radiant, possessed of extraordinary strength, and having a body as firm as a diamond.
Through *saṃyama* on the nature of perception, egoism, inherence, and purposefulness, mastery over the senses is attained.
(Yoga Sūtra 3.47)

The object of apprehension consists of sound and the other sense-objects, which possess the nature of both the universal and the particular; the functioning of the senses toward these objects is "grasping.

This grasping does not take the form of apprehending the universal alone; for if that specific object were not perceived [by the sense], how could it be subsequently determined by the mind through the sense organ?

Furthermore, the nature of the sense organ is a substance—an aggregate of parts inseparably established as both universal and particular—belonging to the *buddhi-sattva*, which is essentially luminous in nature.

The third form among these is the ego (ahaṃkāra), characterized by the sense of "I-am-ness" (asmitā). Its specific manifestations are the sense organs (indriyāṇi). The fourth form consists of the guṇas, which are of the nature of determination and possess the qualities of illumination, activity, and inertia; the sense organs, together with the ego, are the transformation of these guṇas.
The fifth form is that which permeates the guṇas: the state of being directed toward the purpose of the Puruṣa (puruṣārthavattva).
When there is restraint over these five forms of the senses, having achieved mastery in each respective case, the yogin’s mastery of the senses arises from that mastery of the five forms.
From that follows swiftness of mind, the state of being without organs, and mastery over primordial matter (pradhāna).
The unsurpassed attainment of movement for the body is *manojava* (the speed of thought).
The attainment of function by the sense organs of those who are bodiless (*videha*), depending upon the desired place, time, and object, is the state of *vikaraṇa* (transformation).

Mastery over all primary causes and their modifications is the conquest of *pradhāna*. These three perfections are called the "Honey-like" (*madhupratīkā*), and they are attained through mastery over the five forms of the instruments (*karaṇa*).
For one who possesses only the discriminative discernment (*khyāti*) of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, there is sovereignty over all states of being and omniscience.

When the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*), whose impurities of *rajas* and *tamas* have been shaken off, abides in supreme clarity (*vaiśāradya*) and in the highest state known as mastery (*vaśīkāra*), and is established in the form of the mere discernment of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, it attains sovereignty over all states of being.

The meaning is that all the *guṇas*, whose nature consists of both the determining faculty (*vyavasāya*) and the determined object (*vyavaseya*), present themselves to the master—the *kṣetrajña*—as the totality of all that is perceivable.

"Omniscience" means that the discriminative knowledge (*vivekaja-jñāna*) of all the *guṇas* in their entirety—established as having the qualities of the past (*śānta*), the present (*udita*), and the unmanifest (*avyapadeśya*)—is attained without succession.
This is the perfection (*siddhi*) called "Freedom from Sorrow" (*viśokā*), having attained which the yogi dwells as an omniscient one, his bonds of affliction destroyed and himself self-controlled.
From detachment even toward that [guṇas], upon the destruction of the seeds of defects, there is isolation (kaivalya).

When it occurs to him thus: "With the destruction of afflictions and karma, this discriminative cognition is a property of the *sattva*; and the *sattva* has been placed in the category of what is to be abandoned, while the *puruṣa* is immutable, pure, and other than the *sattva*."

Thus, for one who is becoming dispassionate toward this [world], those seeds of affliction—which are like burnt rice seeds and incapable of germination—perish along with the mind (*manas*). When these have dissolved, the person (*puruṣa*) no longer experiences these three types of suffering. Therefore, when these *guṇas*—which had manifested in the mind in the form of the ripening of karma and afflictions and had fulfilled their purpose—return to their source, there occurs for the person an absolute separation from the *guṇas*, which is isolation (*kaivalya*). At that time, the person is simply the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) established in its own nature.
Upon being invited by those who dwell in the higher realms, one should avoid attachment and pride, for otherwise there would be the risk of undesirable consequences.

(YS 3.51) Indeed, there are these four types of yogis: the beginner, the one who has reached the stage of honey, the one whose light is wisdom, and the one who has transcended what is to be cultivated. (YS 3.51)

Among these, the first is the practitioner whose light has merely begun to function; the second possesses "truth-bearing" wisdom (*ṛtaṃbharaprajña*); the third is the conqueror of the elements and the senses, who has performed the protective binding regarding all things already cultivated and those yet to be cultivated, having accomplished what was to be done; as for the fourth, who has transcended all that is to be cultivated, his sole aim is the dissolution of the mind, and his wisdom consists of the sevenfold knowledge of the final stage (*prāntabhūmiprajñā*).

There, when a brahmin realizes the stage called Madhumatī, the resident deities, observing the purity of his being, invite him to their abodes, saying: "O, sit here! Delight yourself here! This enjoyment is desirable; this maiden is desirable; this elixir wards off old age and death; this vehicle travels through the air; these are the wish-fulfilling trees; there is the holy Mandākinī river; the perfected great seers are most excellent and well-disposed; the celestial nymphs are favorable; divine hearing and sight are yours; the body is like a diamond; all this has been acquired by you, long-lived one, through your own virtues. Accept this imperishable, ageless, immortal station, beloved of the gods."

Being addressed in this way, one should contemplate the faults of attachment: "By me, who am being cooked in the terrible coals of cyclic existence and wandering in the darkness of birth and death, this lamp of yoga—which destroys the cataracts of the afflictions—has somehow been obtained. Yet these winds of sensory objects are its adversaries, arising from the womb of craving. Having indeed attained this light, how could I, deceived by this mirage of sense-objects, once again turn myself into fuel for that very same blazing fire of cyclic existence?"

"May there be well-being for you regarding these sense-objects, which are like dreams and are craved by miserable people"—with such a firm resolve, one should cultivate meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Without forming attachments, one should not even feel pride, thinking, "Thus am I sought after even by the gods. For through such pride, one will—due to the conceit of being well-established—not perceive oneself as being seized by the hair by Death.

And thus, heedlessness (*pramāda*), which watches for a lapse, which must be constantly guarded against with effort, having found an opening, will cause the afflictions (*kleśa*) to surge up; from that, the undesirable consequence will follow once again.
Thus, for one who refrains from attachment and pride, the realized goal will become firm and the goal yet to be realized will come into manifestation.
"From *saṃyama* on moments (*kṣaṇa*) and their sequence (*tatkrama*), knowledge born of discrimination arises" (YS 3.52).

Just as the atom (*paramāṇu*) is the ultimate limit of the reduction of substance, so too the moment (*kṣaṇa*) is the ultimate limit of the reduction of time; or rather, that duration of time in which a moving atom leaves its former location and reaches the subsequent location is a moment. The continuity of that flow, however, is "succession" (*krama*). There is no real aggregation of moments and their succession; rather, aggregations such as a *muhūrta*, a day and night, and so forth, are aggregations of the intellect.

Indeed, this time (kāla), though devoid of objective reality, is a mental construction following upon verbal cognition; it appears to ordinary people of emergent vision as if it were the very nature of an object.
But the moment (kṣaṇa) is grounded in reality and is the support of succession, and succession consists in the immediate sequence of moments—this is what the yogis who know time call "time.
Furthermore, two moments do not exist simultaneously, nor is there succession between two co-existent things, because such a thing is impossible.

When there is immediate succession from a preceding moment to a succeeding one, that is "sequence" (*krama*). Therefore, only the present single moment exists; past and future moments do not exist. Consequently, there is no aggregation (*samāhāra*) of them. However, those moments that have passed or will occur must be explained as being endowed with transformation (*pariṇāma*); thus, by means of that single moment, the entire world undergoes transformation.
Indeed, all these phenomena (*dharmas*) are mounted upon that moment. Through *saṃyama* upon both that moment and its sequence, there is direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of them.
And from that, knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*) manifests.
Its specific object is set forth:
"From that, there is the realization of two similar things, because their difference is not delimited by genus, characteristic marks, or location" (YS 3.53).
[YS 3.53] When two things are identical in terms of place and characteristic, the difference in genus (*jāti*) is the cause of their distinction, as in "this is a cow" and "this is a mare.
When they are identical in place and genus, the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is what creates the distinction, as in "the cow Kālākṣī" and "the cow Svastimatī."

Because two *āmalaka* fruits possess a similarity in their generic characteristics (*jāti-lakṣaṇa-sārūpya*), it is the difference in location that creates their distinctness, such as "this is the one in front" and "this is the one behind.

However, when the *āmalaka* fruit that was in front is moved to the position behind while the knower is distracted by something else, then, since they occupy the same location, the distinction—"this is the one in front" and "this is the one behind"—would be untenable.
Since there must be knowledge of reality free from doubt, it has therefore been stated: "From that, comprehension arises through knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*)."

How so? A location co-occurring with a preceding *āmalaka* fruit is distinct from a location co-occurring with a succeeding *āmalaka* fruit; and those two *āmalaka* fruits are distinct due to their experiencing their own respective locations and moments.

Furthermore, the experience of a different location and moment is the cause of their difference. By this example, in the case of an atom whose genus, characteristic, and location are identical [to another], because the succeeding atom does not occupy the same location as the co-occurring moment of the preceding atom’s location, its experience of that location is distinct due to the difference in the co-occurring moment. Thus, for Īśvara or a yogin, there arises the cognition of the difference between those two.

Others, however, explain that those final particularities (*viśeṣa*) produce the cognition of difference; even in that case, the cause of difference consists in the distinction of location, the distinction of form, obstruction, and genus.

But the distinction of moments (*kṣaṇabheda*) is accessible only to the intellect of yogins. Therefore, Vārṣagaṇya said: "Because of the absence of distinctions in form, obstruction, and genus, there is no fundamental separateness. "Born of discrimination (*vivekaja*), knowledge is all-encompassing, has everything as its object, has all modes as its object, and is instantaneous" (Yogasūtra 3.54).

"Star-like" (tāraka) means that which arises from one's own intuition and is not derived from instruction; "having all things as its object" means that there is nothing whatsoever that does not become an object for it.
"Having all modes as its object" means that it knows everything—past, future, and present—in all its various forms and in every way.
"Simultaneous" (*akrama*) means that it grasps everything in every way as mounted upon a single moment.

This is the complete knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*). A portion of this very [knowledge] is the lamp of yoga, beginning from the stage of "Honeyed" (*madhumatī*) until its final completion. [This applies] whether one has already attained the knowledge born of discrimination or has not yet attained it.
"Isolation occurs when there is equality of purity between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*" (YS 3.55).

When the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*), its stains of *rajas* and *tamas* having been shaken off, possesses as its sole remaining function the discernment of its own difference from the *puruṣa*, and the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been burnt away, then it attains, as it were, a state of similarity in purity with the *puruṣa*. At that time, the *puruṣa*'s purity consists in the absence of attributed experience (*upacarita-bhoga*).

In this state, isolation (*kaivalya*) occurs—whether for one who is a Lord or not a Lord, for one who possesses knowledge born of discrimination or otherwise. For one whose seeds of affliction have been burnt, there is no further need for knowledge. This sovereignty and knowledge born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) were introduced as means for the purification of the *sattva*. But in the ultimate sense, through knowledge, non-seeing (*adarśana*) ceases; when that has ceased, the subsequent afflictions do not exist.

Due to the absence of afflictions (*kleśa*), there is an absence of the fruition of karma (*karma-vipāka*). In this state, the qualities (*guṇa*) that were under the jurisdiction of [the *prakṛti*] no longer present themselves to the *puruṣa* as objects of perception.
That is the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the *puruṣa*; then the *puruṣa*, being stainless, becomes solitary (*kevalin*), a light consisting solely of its own essential nature.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Chapter on Powers (*vibhūtipāda*), in the *Vyāsabhāṣya* on the *Yogaśāstra*, the authoritative exposition of Sāṃkhya by the venerable Patañjali.
[The Chapter on Isolation] Perfections arise from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and meditative concentration.
Success through birth is that which is separated from the body, such as [attaining powers] by means of herbs in the abodes of the Asuras or through elixirs (*rasāyana*), and so forth.
Through mantras, there is the attainment of traveling through the sky, the power of atomization (*aṇimā*), and the rest.

Through austerity (*tapas*), there is success through mere volition (*saṃkalpasiddhi*), such as being able to take any form at will and going wherever one desires; these successes born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) have been explained.
In that regard, the transformation of the sense organs of one species into another species occurs through the natural influx of primal matter (prakṛti).
The disappearance of a prior transformation and the emergence of a subsequent transformation occur through the entry of new constituent parts (*avayava*).

Furthermore, the primary natures (*prakṛti*) of the body and the sense organs sustain their respective modifications through replenishment, depending upon causes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth.
"The cause is not the instigator of the primary natures; rather, it effects the removal of obstacles, like a farmer" (Yogasūtra 4.3).

[YS 4.3] For merit and the like are not the motive that impels the primal natures; a cause is not set in motion by its effect. How then? "But from that [merit, etc. comes the breaking of the veil, as in the case of a farmer."

Just as a farmer, wishing to flood another field from a field already full of water, does not draw out the water with his hand—whether the second field be level, lower, or lower still—but rather breaks its embankment; and once that is broken, the waters themselves flow and inundate the other field—so too, *dharma* breaks the obstructive quality of the *prakṛtis*; once that is broken, the *prakṛtis* themselves spontaneously inundate their respective transformations (*vikāras*).

Or, for example, just as that very farmer has no power to force the watery or earthy juices into the roots of the grain in that very field; rather, he merely removes the mudga beans, gavedhukas, śyāmāka millet, and so forth. Once they have been removed, the juices enter the roots of the grain of their own accord. In the same way, dharma is the cause merely for the cessation of adharma, because purity and impurity are absolutely opposed; however, dharma does not become the cause for the natural functioning of primordial nature (prakṛti).

In this regard, Nandīśvara and others are to be cited as examples; likewise, through its opposite, unrighteousness (adharma) also subverts righteousness (dharma), and from that follows the transformation into impurity. In that case as well, Nahuṣa, Ajagara, and others are to be cited as examples.
But when the yogi creates many bodies, are they possessed of a single mind or of multiple minds?—
[The answer is: "The minds of the emanations arise from the mere sense of 'I-ness' (asmitāmātra)" [YS 4.4].
Taking the mere sense of "I-am-ness" (*asmitāmātra*)—the cause of the mind—as its substrate, it creates emanated minds; therefore, they become possessed of consciousness.
Among the various modes of activity, there is a single directing mind for many [emanated minds].
(Yogasūtra 4.5)

How is it that the activity of many minds proceeds preceded by the intention of a single mind? [The yogin] creates a single motivating mind for all the minds; from that, the differentiation of activity arises.
Among these, that which is born of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is without latent impressions (*anāśaya*).
(Yogasūtra 4.6)

The transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) is of five kinds; the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) arise from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Among these, that very mind which is born of meditative absorption is "without latent deposit" (*anāśaya*); for it has no latent deposit, meaning there is no activity of passion and so forth, and thus there is no connection with merit or demerit for the yogin because his afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted. However, for others, there exists a latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*). For this reason—
The karma of the yogin is neither white nor black; for others, it is of three kinds.
Indeed, this fourfold classification of karma consists of the black, the white-and-black, the white, and the neither-white-nor-black.

Among these, the black [karma] belongs to the evil-minded; the white-and-black is accomplished by external means. In that case, the accumulation of the store of karma occurs solely through the gateways of harming others or favoring them. The white [karma] belongs to those engaged in austerity, self-study, and meditation;
for, because it depends entirely upon the mind, it does not require external means and does not come about by harming others.

"Neither white nor black belongs to renunciants whose afflictions have been exhausted and who are in their final bodies. In this context, it is "white" for the yogi alone because of the renunciation of fruits, and "not black" because of the absence of further appropriation; however, for other beings, it is previously stated to be of three kinds.
Therefore, there is the manifestation only of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that are concordant with the ripening of that karma.
(Yogasūtra 4.8)

"From that" means from the threefold karma. "Only those [latencies] which are concordant with its maturation" means that whichever kind of karma has a particular maturation, only those latencies (*vāsanā*) that are concordant with it—which adhere to the maturation of the karma—are manifested. For a celestial (*daiva*) karma undergoing maturation cannot be the cause for the manifestation of latencies pertaining to hell-beings, animals, or humans; rather, only those latencies concordant with the celestial state are manifested. The same analysis applies equally to the cases of hell-beings, animals, and humans.
Even for those [karmic impressions] separated by birth, place, and time, there is immediate succession because memory and latent dispositions (saṃskāra) are of a single nature.
The arising of the fruition of a snake (vṛṣadaṃśa) is manifested when its own manifesting condition appears.

Even if that [latent impression] were separated by a hundred births, or by distance in space, or by a hundred eons, and were to arise again through its own manifesting conditions, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) conditioned by the ripening of the previously experienced tiger would be manifested immediately.

Why? Because even though these [impressions] are separated, a similar action serves as the manifesting cause and becomes the efficient condition; thus, there is indeed immediate succession. And for what reason? Because memory and the latent impressions are of one and the same nature: as the experiences were, so are the latent impressions.

And since these [latent impressions] correspond to the tendencies of karma, and memory arises in accordance with those tendencies, memory proceeds from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) that are separated by birth, place, and time. From memory, in turn, arise further latent impressions; thus, these memories and latent impressions are manifested through the power of the activation of the store of karma (*karmāśaya*). Consequently, even though they are separated [by time], their continuity is established because the relationship between cause and effect is never severed. Furthermore, their beginninglessness is due to the eternity of the desire for life (*āśis*). [Yogasūtra 4.10]
[YS 4.10] Because these desires are eternal, those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are beginningless.
This desire for self-preservation—"May I not cease to be; may I continue to exist"—is observed in everyone; it is not innate.

Why should a creature, as soon as it is born and having never experienced the nature of death, experience fear of death caused by the recollection of the suffering of aversion? Furthermore, an entity that exists by its own nature does not take on a cause.

Therefore, this mind, permeated by beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), acquires certain specific impressions through the power of external signs and turns toward the experience of the person.

Others maintain that the mind, which is subject to contraction and expansion like a lamp within a jar or a palace, possesses a form corresponding merely to the dimensions of the body; in this way, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) are logically possible.

The Teacher [Vasubandhu] holds that it is the very functioning (*vṛtti*) of this all-pervading mind that undergoes contraction and expansion, and that this functioning depends upon causes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth.
The sign (*nimitta*) is twofold: external and internal.
The external depends on physical means such as the body, consisting of praise, giving, salutation, and so forth; the internal, consisting of faith and the like, is dependent on the mind alone.
Thus it has been said: "These abodes of meditators, such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the rest, bring about the preeminent Dharma, being themselves independent of external means."
Of these two, the mental is more powerful.

How so? By what could knowledge and dispassion be surpassed? And who, apart from the power of the mind, would dare to empty the Daṇḍaka forest by physical action alone, or drink up the ocean like Agastya?
Because these [four factors] are comprised of cause, fruit, support, and object, in their absence, those [powers] are absent. (Yogasūtra 4.11)

[YS 4.11] Righteousness (*dharma*) is the cause of pleasure, and unrighteousness (*adharma*) is the cause of pain. From pleasure arises attachment, and from pain arises aversion; from these follows effort, by means of which—through mind, speech, or body—one, while in motion, either benefits or harms another. Therefrom again arise righteousness and unrighteousness, pleasure and pain, and attachment and aversion. Thus this six-spoked wheel of saṃsāra revolves. And for this wheel, which turns at every moment, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the guide and the root of all afflictions (*kleśa*); such is the cause.
As for the fruit, it is that depending upon which a dharma such as [karma] attains its state of being present; for there is no production of what was previously non-existent.
The mind, however, is the basis for the latencies (vāsanās) so long as it possesses its functional capacity (sādhikāra);
for when the mind has ceased its activity, the latencies are unable to remain without a basis.
Whatever object has become manifest manifests whatever latent impression (*vāsanā*); that [object] is its objective support (*ālambana*).

Thus, all latent impressions are subsumed by these four: cause, fruit, basis, and objective support. In the absence of these, there is also the absence of the latent impressions which depend upon them.
Since what is non-existent cannot come into being, and what is existent cannot perish, how can latent impressions—which exist as substantial entities—ever cease?
The past and the future exist in their own nature through the distinction of the temporal paths (*adhvan*) of phenomena (*dharma*).

That whose manifestation is yet to come is the future; that whose manifestation has been experienced is the past; and that which is mounted upon its own activity is the present. These three constitute the object of knowledge for cognition.
If this [past and future] did not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpataḥ*), this cognition would not have arisen as being without an object.
Therefore, the past and the future exist by way of their own intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, if the fruit of karma—whether conducive to experience (*bhoga-bhāgīya*) or conducive to liberation (*apavarga-bhāgīya*)—which is about to arise, were non-existent (*nirupākhya*), then the performance of wholesome deeds for the sake of that [fruit], with that [fruit] as its objective and that [fruit] as its cause, would not be logical.

Furthermore, it is established that a cause is capable of bringing about an existing effect into the present state, rather than producing something previously non-existent; thus, the cause effects a specific favor upon the effect that already exists, rather than generating it anew.

Moreover, the substratum (*dharmin*) possesses the nature of multiple attributes (*dharma*), and these attributes are situated according to their distinction in time-periods (*adhvan*). Now, the past and the future do not exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*) in the same way that the present exists as having attained a specific manifestation. How, then, do they exist? The future exists by its own essential form (*svarūpa*) which is yet to be manifested.

And because it is "past" by virtue of its own nature as a manifested entity, this manifestation of nature belongs only to the present time-path (*adhvan*); it does not exist in the past and future paths.
Furthermore, at the time of one path, two paths are necessarily associated with the substrate (*dharmin*); thus, the three paths do not come into being after having previously been non-existent.
These [paths] are essentially the *guṇas*, whether manifested or subtle.
[YS 4.13] Indeed, these dharmas of the three times— whether present, characterized by manifestation, or past and future, characterized by subtlety— are of six kinds in their undifferentiated forms.
All this is merely a particular arrangement of the *guṇas*; thus, in the ultimate sense, they consist of the *guṇas* themselves.
Accordingly, the instruction of the scripture states:
"The supreme form of the *guṇas* does not come within the range of vision; that which has entered the range of vision is as utterly void as an illusion."
The supreme form of the qualities does not come within the range of vision;
that which has reached the range of vision is utterly void, like an illusion.
But when all are qualities, how can there be one sound and one sense organ?
— Because of the unity of transformation, the reality of the thing is one.

The single transformation of the *guṇas*—which have the natures of manifestation (*prakhyā*), activity (*kriyā*), and stability (*sthiti*), and which consist of the capacity for grasping—is the sense organ, the ear; the single transformation of those [guṇas] which consist of the capacity for being grasped is the object, sound, in the form of the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*). Of sound and the others, which are of the same genus as material form (*mūrti*), the single transformation is the earth atom, which is a constituent part of the subtle element; and the single transformation of these is earth, such as a cow, a tree, or a mountain. In the case of the other elements as well, one should understand that there is a commonality in the commencement of a single modification, based on moisture, heat, motility, and the providing of space.

There is no object that exists apart from consciousness, yet there is knowledge that is imagined to exist apart from an object, as in dreams and the like. Following this line of reasoning, those who deny the intrinsic nature of things—claiming that an entity is merely a mental construction comparable to the objects of a dream and does not exist in ultimate reality—are correct. For how could these people, who by their own power present an object before them, yet discard its very nature through the force of conceptual cognition—which lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge—and then go so far as to deny that very object, be worthy of belief? And why is this [position] improper?
"Because the mind differs despite the identity of the object, the paths of these two are distinct" (YS 4.15).
A single object that serves as the support for many minds is common to all; indeed, it is not imagined by a single mind, nor is it imagined by many minds, but rather it is self-established.

How so? Because there is a difference in the mind despite the identity of the object: even when the object is identical, a cognition of pleasure arises in the mind depending on merit (*dharma*); from that same object, a cognition of pain arises depending on demerit (*adharma*); from that same object, a cognition of delusion arises depending on ignorance (*avidyā*); and from that same object, a cognition of equanimity arises depending on right vision (*samyagdarśana*). By whom, then, is that [object] imagined by the mind?
Furthermore, it is not logical that the coloring of one mind should occur through an object imagined by another mind.
Therefore, there is a distinct path for the object and the cognition, which are differentiated by the distinction between the grasped and the grasper;
there is not even a scent of confusion between these two.

In the Sāṃkhya position, however, the object consists of the three *guṇas* and is mobile, as is the functioning of the *guṇas*; thus, it becomes connected with the mental states (*citta*) in dependence upon causes such as merit (*dharma*).
And as the cognition corresponding to that sign arises, it becomes the cause for that object by means of this or that specific nature.
Some say:

"The object must coexist with the cognition because it is an object of experience, like pleasure and so forth. By this line of reasoning, they refute its commonality [with other cognizers] and thereby deny the very reality of the object in preceding and succeeding moments.
And an object is not dependent on a single mind; otherwise, what would it be when that mind lacks the means of valid cognition?

(YS 4.16) If an object were dependent on a single mind, then when the mind is distracted or suppressed, the object—unperceived by it, having become the non-object of another [mind], lacking any means of valid cognition, and its nature ungrasped by anyone at that time—what would it be? It would be nothing at all.

Furthermore, if it were connected with the mind, from what would it arise? Moreover, those parts of it that are not present would simply not exist for it; thus, if there were no back, the belly could not be perceived either.

Therefore, the object is independent and common to all persons, while the minds are independent and function according to each person; from the connection between these two arises perception, which is the experience of the Puruṣa.
Because the mind depends on being colored by that [Puruṣa], an object is known or unknown. (Yogasūtra 4.17)
[YS 4.17] Objects, which are like magnets, attract the mind, which possesses properties similar to iron, and color it.

That object by which the mind is colored is known; other than that, the object remains unknown. Since an entity thus possesses both a known and an unknown nature, the mind is subject to transformation (pariṇāmin).
But for one for whom that very mind is the object— its fluctuations are always known by its master, the Puruṣa, because of the latter's unchangeability.

If the Puruṣa, like the mind, were subject to transformation, then the mental modifications directed toward him would be sometimes known and sometimes unknown—just as objects such as sound and the rest are. However, the fact that the mind is always known by its master, the Puruṣa, leads one to infer his non-transformative nature. An objection might be raised: "The mind itself may be self-luminous and also manifest objects, just like fire. This is not so; it cannot be self-luminous because it is an object of perception (YS 4.19).
[YS 4.19] Just as the other sense organs and the objects such as sound do not possess their own manifestations because they are objects of perception, so too the mind is to be understood.

Nor is fire a valid example here; for fire does not illuminate its own nature when it is unmanifest, and this illumination is observed only upon the conjunction of the illuminated object and the illuminator.

Furthermore, there is no conjunction in the mere intrinsic nature [of consciousness]. Moreover, the meaning of the word is that the mind, being self-manifesting (*svābhāsa*), is not at all graspable by anything else. For example, the meaning is that space is established in itself and not established in another. The activity of sentient beings is observed to proceed from the experience of the movement of their own intellect—such as "I am angry," "I am afraid," "I have passion for that," or "I have anger toward that. This would not be logical if one's own intellect were not apprehended.
And at one and the same time, there is no simultaneous determination of both [the subject and the object]. (Yogasūtra 4.20)

[YS 4.20] Furthermore, it is not logical for the determination of both its own nature and the nature of another to occur in a single moment; for the proponent of momentariness maintains that whatever is the coming-into-being is itself the action, and that very thing is the agent.
It might be thought: "The mind, having ceased by its own inherent nature, is grasped by a subsequent, immediately preceding mind."
If one mind were perceivable by another mind, there would be an infinite regress of cognitions perceiving cognitions, as well as a confusion of memories.

(YS 4.21) Now, if the mind were to be grasped by another mind, by what would the cognition of that cognition be grasped? That too by another, and that too by another—thus there would be an infinite regress.

Furthermore, there would be a confusion of memories; for as many as are the experiences of cognitions, so many memories would result. And due to that confusion, there would be an inability to determine a single memory. Thus, by the nihilists who deny the existence of the person (*puruṣa*) who experiences cognition, everything has been thrown into disorder.

However, while imagining the nature of the experiencer in various ways, they do not accord with reason. Some, having even postulated a mere "being" (sattva), say, "There exists that being who, having cast off these five aggregates, takes up others," and yet they tremble at that very [conclusion].

Likewise, having said, "I shall lead the holy life in the presence of the Teacher for the sake of great disenchantment with the aggregates, for dispassion, for non-arising, and for peace," they subsequently deny the very existence of that being.
But doctrines such as Sāṃkhya and Yoga, by their own terminology, accept that the *puruṣa* alone is the master and the enjoyer of the mind.
How so?
"The consciousness (*cit*), which does not undergo transition, experiences its own intellect when it assumes the form of that [intellect]" (Yogasūtra 4.22).
[YS 4.22] For the power of the enjoyer is indeed unchanging and non-transmigrating; yet, as if transmigrated into the changing object, it follows its modifications.

And because it merely imitates the modification of the intellect—which has acquired the nature of being assisted by consciousness—the cognitive modification is described as being indistinguishable from the modification of the intellect.
And so it has been said:

"Neither in Pātāla, nor in the clefts of mountains, nor in darkness, nor in the wombs of the oceans, is that cave wherein the eternal Brahman is deposited, which the sages perceive as the undifferentiated activity of the intellect.
Neither in Pātāla, nor in the clefts of mountains, nor in darkness, nor in the wombs of the oceans...
In that cave, the eternal Brahman is deposited, which the seers perceive as the undifferentiated activity of the intellect;
and for this reason it is accepted:
"The mind, colored by both the seer and the seen, has all things as its object" (YS 4.23).

[YS 4.23] For the mind is colored by the object that is to be thought; and because it itself is an object, it is connected with the subject—the Puruṣa—by means of its own function. Thus, this very mind, colored by both the seer and the seen, appearing as both object and subject, having assumed the nature of both conscious and unconscious, though consisting of objects, appears as if it were not an object, though unconscious, as if it were conscious; like a crystal gem, it is said to be "all-purposeful."

Thus, due to this similarity between [the object] and the mind, some are deluded and say that the object itself is consciousness; others say that all this is merely mind (*cittamātra*), and that this world—consisting of cows, jars, and so forth—is indeed without external causes.
These people are to be pitied.
Why? Because they possess the seed of delusion: the notion that the mind manifests in the form of all objective appearances.

In the context of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), the object (*artha*) that has become a reflection is distinct [from wisdom] because it serves as its objective support (*ālambana*).
If that object were merely mind (*cittamātra*), how could the form of wisdom itself be discerned by wisdom alone?
Therefore, the object that has become a reflection within wisdom is that by which it is discerned; that is the *puruṣa*.

Thus, due to the distinction within the mind between the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped, those of right vision distinguish these three according to their respective natures; by them, the Puruṣa is realized.
And why?
Because that [mind], although variegated by innumerable latent impressions (*vāsanās*), exists for the sake of another, since it functions through combination. [Yoga Sūtra 4.24]

[YS 4.24] This mind, though variegated by innumerable latent impressions (*vāsanā*), exists for the sake of another—that is, for the sake of the experience and liberation of another—and not for its own sake, because it functions through association, like a house.

A mind that functions through association cannot exist for its own sake; a pleasant mind is not for the sake of pleasure, nor is knowledge for the sake of knowledge; both of these are for the sake of another.

That person who possesses the purpose consisting of both experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) is indeed the Supreme (*para*), not that which is merely the non-supreme universal (*sāmānyamātra*).

Whatever "supreme" mere universal the Nihilist (*vaināśika*) might cite by way of its own nature, all of that must exist for the sake of another because it functions through combination. But that which is the supreme particular (*viśeṣa*), the Person (*puruṣa*), does not function through combination.
"For one who perceives the distinction, there is the cessation of the cultivation of self-identity" (YS 4.25).

Just as the existence of seeds is inferred by the sprouting of grass during the rainy season, so too, when horripilation and the shedding of tears are observed in someone upon hearing of the path to liberation, it is inferred that there exists within them the seed of the perception of distinction, produced by karma conducive to liberation (*apavargabhāgīya*).

In him, an innate cultivation of self-identity proceeds; due to the absence of which it was said that for those who, setting aside intrinsic nature, take pleasure in the prima facie position regarding faults and the like, and feel aversion toward the final determination, there arises this cultivation of self-identity: "Who was I? How was I? What indeed is this? How indeed is this? Who shall we be? Or how shall we be?"

But that [notion of selfhood] ceases for one who perceives the distinction; for this is merely the manifold transformation of the mind alone, while the Puruṣa, when ignorance is absent, is pure and untouched by the attributes of the mind.
Consequently, the cultivation of the sense of selfhood ceases for the wise man.
At that time, the mind is inclined toward discernment and tends toward isolation (kaivalya). [Yogasūtra 4.26]

At that time, his mind—which had previously been inclined toward objects and submerged in ignorance—becomes otherwise: it becomes inclined toward isolation (*kaivalya*) and submerged in knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*).
In the intervals between these [moments of discriminative knowledge], other cognitions arise from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

[YS 4.27] For the mind that is inclined toward the discernment of cognitive objects and flows solely toward the discriminative awareness of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, other cognitions—such as "I am," or "it is mine," or "I know," or "I do not know"—arise during its intervals.
Why? Because they arise from previous latent impressions whose seeds are being exhausted.
Furthermore, it has been stated regarding these that they are like the afflictions (*kleśa*):

[YS 4.28] "Just as the afflictions, once their seed-nature is burnt, are no longer capable of sprouting, so too the prior latent impression (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), its seed-nature burnt by the fire of knowledge, does not give rise to further cognitions."
However, the purifications of knowledge (jñāna-saṃskāras) are not further considered here, as they follow upon the completion of the mind’s task.

"For one who is free from desire even for contemplation (prasaṃkhyāna), there arises through discriminative discernment (viveka-khyāti) in every respect the concentration called the Cloud of Virtue (dharma-megha-samādhi).

When this Brahmin is not indolent even regarding discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) and therefore desires nothing even from that, then for one who is detached even from that, there arises only the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) in every respect. Because the seeds of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are exhausted, no further cognitions arise for him; at that time, his samādhi is called the "Cloud of Virtue" (*dharmamegha*).
From that follows the cessation of afflictions and karma. [YS 4.30]

[YS 4.30] Through the attainment of that [discriminative discernment], the afflictions such as ignorance are scraped away along with their roots, and the latent deposits of karma—both wholesome and unwholesome—are destroyed along with their very foundations.
When afflictions and karma cease, the wise one becomes liberated even while living. Why? Because error is the cause of worldly existence.
For no one who has exhausted all error is ever seen to be born anywhere by anyone.
At that time, because the knowledge freed from all stains of obscuration is infinite, the knowable is small.
For one who is liberated from all afflictions and karmic obscurations, there is infinity of knowledge.

The infinite essence of knowledge, which is overcome and veiled by obscuring darkness, becomes capable of apprehension only when it is set in motion and opened up in some particular place by passion (*rajas*).
In that regard, when it is freed from all stains of obscuration, then its infinity comes to be.
Because of the infinity of knowledge, the object of knowledge becomes small, like a firefly in the sky.
Regarding this, it is said:
"The blind man pierced the jewel; the fingerless man strung it; the neckless man fastened it on; the tongueless man praised it."
A blind man pierced the jewel; one without fingers strung it;
one without a neck fastened it on; and one without a tongue praised it.
Then, for those who have achieved their purpose, there is the completion of the sequence of transformation of the *guṇas* [YS 4.32].

With the arising of that Cloud of Virtue (*dharmamegha*), the sequence of transformation of the *guṇas* comes to an end for those who have fulfilled their aim; for once enjoyment and liberation have been accomplished and their sequence completed, they are not able to persist even for a moment longer.
Now, what is this so-called "sequence"?
Sequence is that which consists of successive moments, is apprehended through its final limit in a process of transformation, and is perceived by contrast with the preceding moment.
(Yogasūtra 4.33)

Succession (*krama*) is apprehended through the final limit—that is, the termination—of transformation, which consists of moments (*kṣaṇa*) and immediate succession (*ānantarya*). For old age does not occur at the end of a cloth unless the succession of moments has been experienced; furthermore, succession is observed even among eternal things.
This eternity is twofold: immutable eternity (*kūṭasthanityatā*) and transformative eternity (*pariṇāminityatā*).
Among these, the eternity of the *puruṣa* is immutable.

The permanence of the *guṇas* is their state of transformation (*pariṇāminityatā*). That which remains as its own essential nature (*tattva*) even while undergoing transformation is permanent; and because the essential nature of both [the *guṇas* and their modifications] is not destroyed, they possess permanence.

In this regard, the sequence among the qualities of the *guṇas*—such as intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest—which is apprehended by its final limit through transformation, finds its conclusion in the case of the *guṇas* themselves, which are permanent substrates (*dharmin*), whereas it finds no such conclusion in those [modifications].

In the case of liberated persons (*muktapuruṣa*), who are immutably eternal and established solely in their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), the existence of that nature is experienced only sequentially; therefore, even there, [the notion of "is"] is imagined by resorting to the verbal action of "being" through the medium of words, as it does not reach its final limit.
Now, regarding this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) which proceeds through the qualities (*guṇa*) by way of persistence and movement: is there a sequential completion of it or not?

This is an answerable question. How so? The question "Will everyone who is born die? is one to be answered categorically: "Yes, sir. But this [question regarding the end of *saṃsāra*] is not to be answered.
Furthermore, regarding the question, "Will everyone who dies be born again?", this is to be answered by way of analysis (*vibhajya-vacanīya*).
One who has realized true knowledge (*pratyudita-khyāti*), whose craving is exhausted, and who is spiritually skilled will not be born; others, however, will be born.

Likewise, when asked whether the human birth is superior or not superior, such a question is to be answered by way of analysis: it is superior with respect to animals, but it is not so with respect to gods and sages.

However, this question—"Is this saṃsāra finite or infinite?"—is one that should not be answered categorically. For there is an end to the sequence of saṃsāra for the virtuous, but not for the other; thus, there is a fault in restricting it to either alternative. Therefore, this question must indeed be explained [analytically].
When the sequence of the exercise of the guṇas reaches its completion, isolation (kaivalya) is attained; its essential nature is now determined:

"Isolation (*kaivalya*) is the re-absorption (*pratiprasava*) of the *guṇas* that are devoid of purpose for the *puruṣa*, or it is the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) established in its own nature" (YS 4.34).

Isolation is the re-absorption of the *guṇas*—which consist of both effects and causes and are now devoid of purpose for the *puruṣa* since enjoyment and liberation have been accomplished. Furthermore, being established in its own nature means that, due to the absence of any further connection with the *buddhi-sattva*, the *puruṣa* is nothing but the power of consciousness alone; its remaining forever in that very state is isolation.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Kaivalya-pāda, in the Yoga-śāstra known as the Sāṃkhya-pravacana, the commentary by Vyāsa on the venerable Pātañjala [Yoga-sūtra].
